en: The year is indeed the sacrifice, Prajāpati; its door is this new moon (amāvāsyā), and the moon itself is the door-bolt.

He who establishes the two fires on the day of the new moon is like one who would enter a city through an open door. 11.1.1 [2] He who establishes the two fires on the day of the new moon is like one who would enter a city through an open door. From that [he prospers].
In this very way one goes to the heavenly world; such is the case for him who establishes the sacred fires on the new moon day.
Now, he who establishes them under a lunar mansion (nakṣatra) is like one who would attempt to enter a city through a gate that has been closed; he would approach the city crookedly.
Such is the case for him who establishes them under a lunar mansion; therefore, one should not establish the fires under a lunar mansion.
On the day when he is seen neither in front nor behind, on that day one should fast; for on that occasion he comes to this world and dwells here in it.
All the gods dwell there, all beings, all deities, all seasons, all hymns, and all [sacrificial elements]. 11.1.1. [5]
All the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras] are the *candas*.
Indeed, in all the gods, in all beings, in all deities, in all seasons, in all *stomas*, in all *pṛṣṭhas*, and in all *candas*, the two fires are established for him.

He who establishes the sacred fires on the new moon day should establish the two fires on that very new moon day. That new moon day which occurs in the month of Vaiśākha—one should establish the fires on that day; it coincides with Rohiṇī. The self is indeed offspring and cattle; Rohiṇī is the self.
Thus, he becomes firmly established in his own self, in offspring, and in cattle. Or rather, [it is] the new moon day.
Therefore, the form of the *agnyādheya* (the laying of the fires) is such that one should establish the two fires on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) itself;
one should take hold [of the ritual] on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*), and be initiated (*dīkṣeta*) on the new moon day.
They indeed slay this sacrifice when they perform it; for when they press the King [Soma], they [slay him]. 11.1.2. [1] It is he whom they slay.
When they kill the sacrificial animal, when they quiet it, and when they dissect it—that is what they kill it for.
By means of the mortar and pestle, and by means of the lower and upper grinding stones, they kill the *havis*-sacrifice.
Having killed that sacrifice, he pours it as seed into the fire, which is its womb; for fire is indeed the womb of the sacrifice. From that [it arises].

It is born; one should therefore accomplish those ten oblations for which the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered. This sacrifice is indeed he who blows here (the wind); he blows as if he were one alone, yet having entered into man, he is distributed tenfold. Thus, through these prepared vital breaths (*prāṇas*), he is born from the womb of Agni. This is that *virāj* consisting of ten syllables.

This indeed is the perfection, this is the sacrifice. Or there may be nine; he thereby makes the Virāj deficient for the sake of procreation, for from a deficiency these creatures are born. This indeed is the perfection, this is the sacrifice.

Moreover, if there should be one extra [verse], it exceeds Prajāpati; this is that perfection, this is the sacrifice. (11.1.2.6) Moreover, if there should be two extras, a pair is indeed a productive couple; thus a productive couple is thereby created. This is that perfection, this is the sacrifice. (11.1.2.7)

Moreover, there may also be three extra [verses]; that makes a pair, a productive union; and what is born therein is the third—this is the perfection, this is the sacrifice. Furthermore, there may also be four extra [verses]; for just as one is, so are four; and since these worlds are three, they are indeed these very worlds.

Through three [verses] one attains the worlds; Prajāpati, indeed, is the fourth beyond these worlds. Thus, by means of the fourth, one attains Prajāpati himself. This is the perfection, this is the sacrifice. That which is deficient by two is deficient; that is not a sacrifice. That which exceeds by five exceeds; that is not a sacrifice.

This very same [series] extends beyond to ten; this to twenty; this to a thousand. (11.1.2) Those who sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices run a race. He should indeed sacrifice for fifteen years.
In those fifteen years, there are three hundred and sixty full moons and new moons.
There are indeed three hundred and sixty nights in a year; he thus attains those nights. 11.1.2.
[11] Then, for another fifteen years he should sacrifice. Of those fifteen years, there are three hundred and sixty full-moon and new-moon days; indeed, there are three hundred and sixty.
The days of the year—those very days he attains, and through them he indeed attains the year.
In the beginning, the gods were mortal; as soon as they attained the year, they became immortal.
The year is indeed everything, and everything is imperishable. By this, his merit becomes imperishable, and his world becomes imperishable.
He alone is the foremost among those who rush to battle who, knowing thus, performs sacrifice for thirty years; therefore, one should indeed sacrifice for thirty years.
However, if he should be a performer of the Dākṣāyaṇayajña, then he may also sacrifice for fifteen years, for in this way that ritual perfection is attained:
he sacrifices at two full-moon festivals and two new-moon festivals; it is precisely here that [the perfection] is realized.

That becomes prosperity: having sacrificed with the Full-moon sacrifice, he subsequently prepares an offering for Indra Vimṛdh; he sacrifices with that in the same manner as the primary sacrifice. Having sacrificed with the New-moon sacrifice, he subsequently prepares a pap for Aditi; he sacrifices with that in the same manner as the primary sacrifice.
When, having sacrificed with the Full-moon offering, he subsequently offers to Indra Vimṛdh, Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice;
yet, since the Full-moon oblation belongs to Agni and Soma, nothing there is done with the formula "To Indra thee.
By this [subsequent offering], his oblation becomes possessed of Indra, and by this, the sacrifice itself becomes possessed of Indra. Then, as for the words "To Vimṛdh thee":
For indeed, by means of the Full Moon sacrifice, one slays all enemies and destroyers.

Now, when one has sacrificed with the New Moon [offering], he subsequently prepares a pap for Aditi. This King Soma is indeed the food of the gods, which is the moon; and on that night when he is seen neither in the east nor in the west—
Therefore, this oblation becomes as it were unsubstantial, and for that reason it is without a firm foundation. This earth, indeed, is Aditi; she is manifest, and she is firmly established.

By means of this [offering], his oblation becomes as it were substantial, and by means of this it becomes firmly established. Now, as to why he offers the after-offerings (*anuyāja*s), and why he should not offer them. 11.1.3. [4]

When, having sacrificed with the Full-moon offering, he subsequently prepares an oblation for Indra Vimṛdh, thinking, "May my sacrifice be possessed by Indra," then since the entire sacrifice belongs to Indra alone, by this means his sacrificial oblation becomes possessed by Indra, and by this means his sacrifice becomes possessed by Indra. 11.1.3. [5]
Now, as for the fact that after performing the New Moon sacrifice, one subsequently offers a pap to Aditi: the subsequent offering belongs to the New Moon.
Or rather, it was on the Full Moon day that Indra slew Vṛtra; therefore, when he had slain Vṛtra, the gods subsequently offered this oblation for him, which is the New Moon sacrifice.
Why, then, should one offer a subsequent offering at a subsequent offering?
One should not offer them as secondary oblations (anunirvapa).
When, having sacrificed with the Full-moon offering, one offers another oblation; or when, having sacrificed with the New-moon offering, one offers another oblation—one [thereby] serves his enemy.

He rises up against his rival; but he who sacrifices with the Full Moon [oblation] on the Full Moon day and with the New Moon [oblation] on the New Moon day, his prosperity becomes truly unassailable and free from rivals.
For by sacrificing with the Full Moon [rite] on the Full Moon day and with the New Moon [rite] on the New Moon day, the gods indeed quickly [attained their goal].

They struck away evil and were swiftly procreated. He who, knowing thus, performs the Full Moon sacrifice on the day of the full moon and the New Moon sacrifice on the day of the new moon, swiftly strikes away evil and is swiftly procreated.
If he should offer the subsequent oblations, he should give a sacrificial fee; for there should be no oblation without a fee.
Regarding this, they say: "The *anvāhārya* is indeed the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

Now, concerning the *anunirvāpya* (the subsequent offering) and the *abhyudita* (the sacrifice performed when the moon has risen): some, having seen [the moon], observe the fast, thinking, "It will not rise tomorrow," whether because of clouds or because it is not clearly perceived.
They dwell near the wind, and then the sun rises over him. If the sun should rise while the oblation has not yet been taken out, that is well known:

they perform the same observance as before; they take the milk of the previous day and make it into curds for the mixing of the oblation; they release the calves, and then drive them back again. 11.1.4. [2]
In the afternoon, he drives them away with a leafy branch. This is exactly like that well-known New Moon oblation;
however, if one does not intend to observe the vow or if the moon should rise while the oblation has already been taken, then it is otherwise.
He should prepare these very same rice grains after having husked them; those that are the smallest, he bakes into an eight-potherd cake (*puroḍāśa*) for Agni Dātṛ.
Then, as for the milk and curds prepared on the previous day, those are for Indra Pradātṛ; and the milk milked at that very time is for Viṣṇu.

For Śipiviṣṭa, he cooks this rice-oblation (caru) in a vessel of *cūta* wood; for it is indeed a *caru* wherever they pour out the rice grains. Now, as to why it is thus: this is King Soma, the food of the gods.
That which the moon has gone to set, that he has won; Agni, the giver, gives it to him; Indra, the bestower, presents it to him.
Indra and Agni give that sacrifice to him; with that sacrifice given by Indra and Agni, he sacrifices. Now, as for "to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa": Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; and as for "Śipiviṣṭa."
Whatever he approaches, that he reaches; it becomes, as it were, the "Cipita" (the flattened) part of the sacrifice. Therefore [he says], "to Cipiviṣṭa.
In that case, he should give whatever he is able to afford, for they say, "The oblation must not be without a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Then, when the moon does not rise, on that day he should fast. 11.1.5. [1]
Thinking "today is the new moon," he observes the fast; yet this [moon] is seen afterwards. This is indeed the celestial dog;
it looks upon the cattle of the sacrificer, which would be detrimental to his cattle if no expiation were performed. It is out of fear of this very moon that they do so. 11.1.5. [2]
They approach the shadow; by this they call it "the scorched" (*upatapad*), and by this they call it "the dog-licked" (*śvalucita*). 11.1.5.
[3] "The hare-marked moon" (*śaśacāndramasa*): Soma is indeed the moon, the food of the gods; him—
They press [the Soma] on the full-moon day. During the waning half of the month, the moon enters the waters and the plants; for cattle eat both water and plants.
Thus, on that night, he brings it together for the sake of the cattle.
Thinking, "Today is the new-moon day," he observes the fast; then, when this [moon] is seen in the west, the sacrificer [proceeds].
He departs from the path of the sacrifice. Regarding this they say: "How should one act? Should he sacrifice after having departed from the path of the sacrifice, or should he not sacrifice?
One should indeed sacrifice; for there is no other way of departing. Day after day he rises as something superior.
Having sacrificed according to the procedure of the new moon (āmāvāsya), he then performs a subsequent offering (anunirvapati). That may be on that very day or on the following day.

For this [sacrifice], there are three oblations: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Pathikṛt (the maker of the path), a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra Vṛtrahan (the slayer of Vṛtra), and a cake on twelve potsherds for Agni Vaiśvānara.
When he offers to Agni Pathikṛt, Agni is indeed the maker of the path; therefore, from whichever [path] the sacrificer here [sets out]...
He departs from the path of the sacrifice; Agni leads him back onto that very path.

Now, as for [the offering] to Indra Vṛtrahan: Vṛtra is indeed evil, he who stands obstructing prosperity from auspicious and righteous action; this [offering] slays that evil Vṛtra by means of Indra himself, the slayer of Vṛtra.
Therefore, [he offers] to Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra. Now, as for the fact that he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara:
when Indra slew Vṛtra, he completely consumed him with Agni Vaiśvānara; thus, his entire evil [was destroyed].
In the same way, having slain the evil Vṛtra with Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, he now completely burns it away with Agni Vaiśvānara;
thus he completely burns away all his evil. And whoever, knowing this, performs this sacrifice—verily, not even the slightest evil remains over for him. 11.1.5. [9]

For this [offering], there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; he sacrifices to the deities in a whisper; whichever [deities] he desires, those he makes into the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses; likewise for the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, and likewise for the two *saṃyājyā* verses.
He gives a bow with three arrows as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); for with a bow they ward off dogs; thus, by this, he wards off this very one (the dog).
That he gives three bows as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
He gives a staff as the sacrificial fee; for with a staff they ward off dogs, and so by giving a staff as the sacrificial fee, he wards this one [the dog] off.
This is the prescribed sacrificial fee; however, he should also give something else in addition to it, whatever other [gifts] there may be.
Whatever sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) may accrue for them, this is indeed that animal sacrifice; even if it has not been specifically prescribed, one should certainly perform it.

In the beginning, this universe was indeed only water, a mere ocean. It desired: "How might we be reproduced? They exerted themselves; they practiced austerity. While they were practicing austerity, a golden egg came into being within them; it was born.
At that time, there was only the year; this golden egg floated about for as long as the duration of a year.
Then, at the end of a year, a person came into being; he was Prajāpati. Therefore, it is only after a year that a woman or...

Whether it be a cow or a mare, she brings forth her offspring after a year; for Prajāpati was born after a year. He burst open this golden egg, yet at that time there was no resting place whatsoever. Bearing that very golden egg, he floated about for as long as the duration of a year. 11.1.6 [3]

He desired to expand during the year; he uttered "bhūḥ," and this earth became [bhūḥ]; he uttered "bhuvaḥ," and that intermediate space became [bhuvaḥ]; he uttered "svaḥ," and yonder sky became [svaḥ]. Therefore, it is only after a year that a child desires to crawl, for Prajāpati uttered [the vyāhṛtis] after a year.
Indeed, when Prajāpati first spoke, he spoke only monosyllables and disyllables; therefore, a child, when speaking for the first time, speaks only monosyllables and disyllables. 11.1.6 [5]

Or rather, these five syllables he made into the five seasons; these are the five seasons. Thus, when these worlds had been born, Prajāpati arose within a year. Therefore, a child should rise up at a year of age, for Prajāpati arose at a year of age. 11.1.6. [6]
He was born with a lifespan of a thousand years; just as one might behold the far shore of a river, he beheld the far shore of his own life.
Desiring offspring, he moved about worshipping and exerting himself. He deposited his procreative power within himself alone; he [did so] by means of his mouth alone.

He created the gods; those gods were created reaching toward heaven. That they were created reaching toward heaven is the godhood of the gods. For him who was being created, it became as if day; that indeed is the godhood of the gods, in that for him who was being created it became as if day. 11.1.6 [8]
Then, by means of this downward breath, he created the Asuras; they were created having descended upon this very earth.

For him, as he was creating them, it became as if darkness. He thought: "I have indeed created evil, for as I was creating them, it became as if darkness. From that very point, he [turned away from] them.

They pierced them with evil; from that very cause they were defeated. Therefore they say: "There is no such thing as a conflict between gods and Asuras, except for what is recounted in narrative and legend. For it was from that very cause that Prajāpati pierced them with evil, and from that very cause they were defeated. 11.1.6. [10]

Therefore, this was declared by the seer: "You do not wish to fight on any day whatsoever; O Maghavan, you have no enemy at all. That which they call your battles is merely illusion; today you do not wish to fight an enemy, nor indeed in the past. 11.1.6 [11]

When he had created the gods, there was light for him; he made that into the day. Then, when he had created the Asuras, there was darkness for him; he made that into the night. These two became day and night.
11.1.6. [12] Prajāpati reflected: "I have indeed moved through everything, since I have created these deities. He...

He became the year; for "year" (saṃvatsara) is indeed the name of this very thing which is called the year. Whoever thus knows this "year-ness" of the year—whatever evil seeks to pursue him by means of illusion, it does not overcome him; rather, he overcomes whoever seeks to practice sorcery against him.
Thus one knows the yearliness of the year. 11.1.6 [13] Prajāpati thought: "I have created this, the year, as a likeness of myself.
Therefore they say, "Prajāpati is the year," for he created this as a likeness of himself. Furthermore...

The year has four syllables, and Prajāpati has four syllables; therefore, he is indeed his counterpart. These deities were created from Prajāpati: Agni, Indra, Soma, and Parameṣṭhin, the son of Prajāpati.

They were born with a lifespan of a thousand years; just as one might see the far shore of a river, they beheld the far shore of their own lifespan. 11.1.6. [16] They moved about singing and toiling; then Parameṣṭhin, the son of Prajāpati, [appeared].

He beheld the sacrifice, namely the New and Full Moon sacrifices; he sacrificed with them. Having sacrificed with them, he desired, "May I alone be all this. He became the waters; for the waters indeed are all this. Whatever stands in the highest place, if one were to dig here, one would find only water, for it is from the highest [place].
Because it rains from this place in heaven, it is therefore called *parameṣṭhī*.

That *parameṣ�ṭhī* said to his father Prajāpati, "I have seen a sacrifice that fulfills all desires; with that, I shall perform a sacrifice for you. "So be it," [Prajāpati replied]. He performed the sacrifice for him. Having sacrificed, he desired, "May I alone be all this. He...
He became the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Indeed, this whole world is the vital breath; this vital breath is Prajāpati—he who blows here.
His vision is this: "He blows thus. Whatever breathes, that is Prajāpati. He who knows this vision of Prajāpati truly becomes, as it were, manifest. 11.1.6 [18]

That Prajāpati said to his son Indra, "Let me cause you to sacrifice with this wish-fulfilling sacrifice, by means of which the Parameṣṭhin sacrificed for me here. "So be it," he replied. He caused him to sacrifice. Having sacrificed, he desired, "May I alone be all this. He became Speech; for Speech indeed is all this. Therefore they say, "Indra is Speech. 11.1.6 [19]

Indra said to his two brothers, Agni and Soma, "Let me cause you both to sacrifice with this sacrifice that fulfills desires—the very one with which my father Prajāpati sacrificed for me. They replied, "So be it," and he caused them to sacrifice. Having sacrificed, they both desired, "May we alone become all this. For them, there was a consumer of food...
Thus one became the food and the other the eater of food; Agni became the eater of food and Soma the food.
Indeed, all this is both food and the eater of food. These five deities performed this sacrifice, which fulfills desires. Whatever desires they had when they sacrificed, that [was fulfilled].
From these, their desire was fulfilled; for whatever desire one sacrifices with this sacrifice, that desire is fulfilled for him.
Having sacrificed, they beheld the eastern direction; they made it the east, and thus it remains the east.

Therefore these creatures crawl forward; for they made this [direction] forward, thinking, "Let us make this one from here. They made it *ūrj* (nourishment); they thought, "May we behold this very *ūrj*. That became yonder sky. Then they saw the southern direction;
they made that very [direction] the southern. Therefore this is indeed the southern direction (*dakṣiṇā*). Therefore...

From the south alone they attend upon the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās), and from the south they drive them away; for [they thought], "Since we have not made these [gifts] here, let us now make them here. They made that world, thinking, "Let us see this world indeed. That became this intermediate space (antarikṣa); for this is indeed that world. And as this [earth] is...
The earth is the foundation in this world; even so, this intermediate space is the foundation in that world.
Since one who is here does not see that world, therefore they say, "That world is beyond the range of sight. 11.1.6. [23]

Then they beheld the western direction and made it their hope (*āśā*). Therefore, whatever one finds after going eastward, one reaches that very direction by it; for they made this [west] their hope, thinking, "Let us make this one even closer. They made it prosperity (*śrī*), thinking, "May we behold this prosperity. This became the earth; for this earth is indeed prosperity. Therefore, whoever possesses most of it—
He alone finds it; he becomes the most excellent.

11.1.6.[24] Then, looking toward the northern direction, they made it water, thinking, "Let us prepare this for him. They performed that rite (*dharma*); indeed, water is *dharma*. Therefore, whenever waters come to this world, all of this [becomes] entirely so.
It becomes according to dharma; now, when there is drought, the stronger indeed takes from the weaker, for water is dharma.
These, then, are the eleven deities: five fore-offerings (prayāja), two butter-portions (ājyabhāga), the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, and three after-offerings (anuyāja).
These are the eleven oblations. By these oblations, indeed, the gods conquered these worlds and these quarters;

and so also does this [sacrificer] by these oblations conquer these worlds and these quarters. 11.1.6. [27] There are four intermediate directions; those same four *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings are the intermediate directions. For the gods, by means of four [offerings], [conquered] the intermediate directions.
By means of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, the gods conquered the intermediate quarters;
verily, by these [offerings], this sacrificer likewise conquers them. Now, with the *iḍā*, the gods conquered food; likewise, by this [offering], this sacrificer likewise conquers food.
This, indeed, is the perfection of the New and Full Moon sacrifices with respect to the deities.
Now, with respect to the self: these five vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person, excluding the two eyes, are themselves the five fore-offerings (*prayāja*).
The two eyes are the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*).
This downward breath (*avāṅ prāṇa*) is the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; for he offers it as if somewhat less than the other oblations.

Therefore, all the vital breaths recoil from this vital breath; and because he cuts portions for the *sviṣṭakṛt* from all the oblations, therefore whatever comes upon these vital breaths, all that converges into this very one.
There are three phalli; they are those same three *anuyāja* offerings. That which is the most excellent *anuyāja* is this—
"One should recite that [section] without taking breath, as if it were the most excellent member," so they say; "in this way, indeed, it becomes unassailable for him.
He should indeed breathe once, for this has but one joint; and as for that which is without a joint, he should either recite it continuously or...
It may either stand or hang down; therefore this [breath] both stands and moves downward. Therefore, one should blow upon it only once.
(11.1.6.33) The two arms and the two thighs—these are the four *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. This very breath is the foundation, and the *iḍā* is that breath.
Because he does not offer it into the fire, and because it is as if not burnt up, therefore this breath is unobstructed. (11.1.6.34)

The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses are indeed the bones, and the oblation (*havis*) is the flesh; this is measured by the *chandas*. Since the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* are [the bones], therefore the bones remain equal in size whether the person is fat or thin. But because he takes up the oblation both more and less, therefore the flesh becomes fat when the person is fat, and the flesh becomes thin when the person is thin.

Therefore, by means of this sacrifice, he worships whichever deity he desires, for whom there is an oblation. These indeed are the oblations that are not to be omitted. For if he were to omit any of these, it would be as if he were to crush a limb or strike away a vital breath.
Other oblations indeed are brought forward and carried away.
These, then, are sixteen offerings; for man consists of sixteen parts, and the sacrifice is man; therefore there are sixteen offerings.

Regarding that very matter, it is said at the commencement of the vow: "If he does not eat, he belongs to the ancestors; if he does eat, he eats beyond the gods. Therefore, they establish the rule: "He should eat forest-grown food.
If he eats cultivated plants, he eats the essence of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*); if he eats wild plants, [he eats the essence of the wild grains].

If he eats the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he consumes its essence; if he eats [food] from a wooden vessel, he consumes the essence of the fuel-wood (*idhma*); if he drinks milk, he consumes the essence of the *sāṃnāyya* and the clarified butter (*ājya*); if he drinks water, he consumes the essence of the *praṇītā* waters; if he does not eat at all, he becomes one whose deity is the ancestors (*pitṛdevatya*). 11.1.7. [3]

Regarding this they ask: "What is the support? One should oneself indeed perform the *agnihotra* for these two nights. In that he eats after having offered, by that he does not become one whose deity is the Pitṛs; for this is an oblation (*āhuti*). In that he offers this very oblation within himself, by that he does not eat of these sacrificial portions (*medha*). 11.1.7 [4]

Indeed, all nights converge in these [two] nights: those nights of the waxing fortnight all converge in the full-moon night, and those nights of the waning fortnight all converge in the new-moon night. He who, knowing this, himself offers the oblation on the fast-day—verily, for him it is always offered by himself.

It becomes an offering (huta). 11.1.8.[1] Both the gods and the asuras, the offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another. Then the asuras, through sheer arrogance, thought, "In what [mouth] shall we offer? and they proceeded offering into their own mouths; it was indeed through that very arrogance.

They were defeated; therefore, one should not be arrogant, for arrogance is the very gateway to defeat. 11.1.8.[2] Then the gods proceeded, each offering oblations into the other; to them Prajāpati gave himself, for sacrifice was theirs—sacrifice, indeed, is the food of the gods. 11.1.8.[3]
Having offered himself to the gods, he then created this image of himself, namely the sacrifice;
therefore they say, "Prajāpati is the sacrifice," for he created this as an image of himself.
By means of this sacrifice, he ransomed himself from the gods. When he undertakes the vow, it is just as...

Prajāpati offered himself to the gods; in the very same way, this sacrificer now offers himself to the gods. Therefore, he should conduct himself with self-restraint during that night, just as one would conduct oneself with an oblation, for he becomes an oblation for the gods. 11.1.8 [5]

Now, when he performs the sacrifice, it is by means of the sacrifice itself that he ransoms himself from the gods, just as Prajāpati ransomed himself. Then, when he offers the oblation, it is by means of the oblation that he ransoms the sacrifice:
the oblation by the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*), the invitatory verse by the portioning (*avadāna*), the portioning by the offering verse (*yājyā*), and the offering verse by the *vaṣaṭ*-call.
By means of the *vaṣaṭ*-call, the oblation is not yet redeemed; its oblation remains unredeemed.
Just as a tree that has fallen at its very top, so does his sacrifice become. He redeems the oblation by means of the *anvāhārya* (the mess of rice).
Because he brings back (*anvāharati*) that which was deficient in the sacrifice, it is called *anvāhārya*. Thus...
This entire sacrifice becomes ransomed through laughter; for this sacrifice indeed becomes the self of the sacrificer in that world beyond.
He who, knowing this, performs the sacrifice as a ransoming, is born in that world beyond with his whole body intact. 11.2.1. [1]

A man is indeed born thrice. First, he is born from his mother and father; then, when the sacrifice approaches him and he performs it, he is born for the second time; and when he dies, where they place him upon the fire, and when he arises therefrom, he is born for the third time. Therefore, [it is performed] thrice.
"They say, 'A person is born.

11.2.1.[2] He recites these eleven *sāmidhenī* verses. There are indeed ten vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person, and the self (*ātman*) is the eleventh, in which these vital breaths are established. A person is indeed of this extent; thus he causes him to be born complete. And then...
That which follows the *sāmidhenī* verses is the foundation; having thus brought him forth, he establishes him upon that foundation.
There are nine utterances (*vyāhṛti*) of procreation, for there are vital breaths in the ninth generation of man; thus he brings him forth for a second time.
The call for the *āśrāvaṇa* and the response of the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* constitute the foundation. Now, that which was previously mentioned regarding birth in the context of creation—

Thus he produces him for the third time; the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings themselves are the foundation therein. For a man is indeed born three times; in this very way, he thus produces him three times from the sacrifice. Of those eleven [verses], he recites the first one three times and the last one three times.

These are the fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses; two *āghāra* libations; five *prayāja* offerings; the *iḍā*; three *anuyāja* offerings; the *sūktavāka*; and the *śamyorvāka*—these constitute thirteen oblations. Then there is that which he takes up together during the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, and the *samiṣṭayajus*. 11.2.1 [6]

These are the fifteen oblations; for these fifteen oblations, these are the invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*); these fifteen are the kindling verses (*sāmidhenī*); for these invitatory verses, these are the offering verses (*yājyā*). Whatever mantra or *nigada* occurs here, that has the form of an offering verse. By this means, indeed, his oblations become possessed of invitatory verses through these [verses].

By means of these *sāmidhenī* verses, these oblations become accompanied by both *anuvākyās* and *yājyās*. He recites a *gāyatrī* as the *anuvākyā*; for the *gāyatrī* has three feet, and these worlds are three; thus the gods established these very worlds.

Then he sacrifices with a *triṣṭubh* verse. The *triṣṭubh* indeed has four feet, and cattle have four feet; thus the gods established cattle themselves in these worlds that were already firmly established. The *vaṣaṭ*-call consists of two syllables, and man is two-footed; thus they placed this two-footed man among these four-footed cattle.
When [the worlds] were established, he established [them]. This two-footed person is established among the animals; in this very way, he establishes these worlds.
When the worlds are established, he establishes the animals; when the animals are established, he establishes himself.
In this way, this man establishes himself among the cattle—he who, knowing thus, performs the sacrifice.

Now, when he offers at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, that which blazes yonder is indeed the *vaṣaṭ*-call; it is Death. Thus he prepares him above Death, and thereby he causes him to be born from that. He [the sacrificer]—this one...
He is released from death. Indeed, the sacrifice becomes his self;
thus, having become the sacrifice itself, he is released from this death. By this, all his sacrificial rites are released from this death.
Now, this oblation which he offers—this oblation indeed becomes his self in yonder world. He...
When one who is thus prepared departs from this world, then this oblation calls him from behind, saying, "Come!
I am indeed your self here. Because it calls (āhvayati), it is therefore called an oblation (āhuti).
In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman; it created the gods. Having created the gods, [it placed them] in these worlds.
He caused Agni to ascend in this very world, Vāyu in the intermediate space, and Sūrya in the sky.

Then, as for those worlds that are above these, he caused those deities who are above these [worlds] to ascend into them. Just as these worlds here are manifest and these deities are manifest, even so are those worlds manifest and those deities manifest in which those deities reside.
He caused [them] to ascend.

Then Brahman alone went to the further shore (*parārdha*). Having reached that further shore, he reflected: "How indeed might I descend again to these worlds? He descended by means of two things alone: by form (*rūpa*) and by name (*nāman*).
Whatever has a name, that is its name; and even that which has no name, which one knows by its form as "this is its form"—that is its form.
This whole world consists of just this much: namely, form and name. These two are the great powers (*abhva*) of Brahman. He who knows these two great powers of Brahman—

It becomes truly great and vast. These two are indeed the two great mysteries (*yakṣa*) of Brahman. He who knows these two great mysteries of Brahman becomes truly a great mystery himself. Of these two, one is superior: namely, Form; for even Name is [dependent upon] it.

That is indeed form. For he who knows the superior of these two becomes superior to that from which he desires to become superior. 11.2.3. [6] Mortals, indeed, were the gods in the beginning. When they attained the *brahman*, then they became immortal. That which he pours out with the mind—form is indeed the mind, for by the mind one knows, "This is form. Through that, he obtains form; and that which...

He pours an oblation of speech; for "name" is indeed speech, since by means of speech one grasps a name, and thereby one obtains the name. This entire world is as much as form and name; he thus obtains all this. All is indeed inexhaustible;
by this, his merit becomes inexhaustible, and his world becomes inexhaustible. 11.2.3. [7]
Now, this very thing is undertaken with a verse addressed to Agni, just as the sacrifice became pleasing to the Ṛṣis and they performed it accordingly.

While the Ṛṣis were performing that sacrifice, the Gandharvas sat down near them; they would observe them, saying, "In this they have exceeded," or "In this they have made a deficiency. When their sacrifice was completed, then he showed it to them.
They said, "They have made this either excessive or deficient.
Now, that which they made excessive was like mountains; and that which they made deficient was like chasms and ravines.
When he utters the *śamyor*, he touches it [the sacrificial post], saying: "O Sacrifice, homage to thee! And do thou rest in the auspiciousness of the sacrifice;
mayst thou rest in my well-offered sacrifice. By this word "homage," he pacifies whatever he has exceeded;
and by the word "and [rest]," that which he has made deficient becomes non-deficient in the auspiciousness of the sacrifice.

"Be completed," he says; for whatever is deficient or excessive in the sacrifice is ill-omened (*sviṣ*), and by this [formula] he pacifies both of those. "Be well-sacrificed and be completed for me," he says; for whatever is deficient or excessive in the sacrifice is well-sacrificed (*sviṣṭa*), and by this he pacifies both of those.
Thus, indeed, his sacrifice becomes one that is neither deficient nor excessive, for him who knows thus.
The wise man touches it thus; therefore, one should touch it in this very way. Now, those Gandharvas were Āsuḥ, Śūrpa, Yavāman, Kṛṣi, Udvalavan, and Dhānāntarvan. 11.2.4.
[1] This one who shines yonder is indeed the Full Moon (Pūrṇamās), for he is filled day after day; and he is also the New Moon (Darśa).
"That which is the moon is indeed the *darśa* (the new moon), for it is as if seen (*dṛśya*) here. Moreover, they say otherwise: "The full moon itself is the *pūrṇamā* (the full moon);
for following its filling, they call it *paurṇamāsī* (the full-moon day). And this very sun is the *darśa*, for he is as if seen (*dṛśya*) here."

This very [earth] is the full moon, for she is indeed full; yonder sky is the new moon, for yonder sky is, as it were, visible. Night is the full moon, for this night is indeed full; day is the new moon, for this day is, as it were, visible.
This, then, is the investigation regarding the Full Moon and New Moon sacrifices among the gods.
Now, with reference to the self: the *udāna* breath is indeed the *Pūrṇamāsī*, for by the *udāna* this person is, as it were, filled.
The *prāṇa* breath is indeed the *Darśa*, for this *prāṇa* is, as it were, seen. Thus, these two—the eater of food and the giver of food—are the *Darśa* and *Pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices.
The *prāṇa* is the eater of food, for by the *prāṇa* this food is eaten; the *udāna* is the giver of food, for by the *udāna*—
"Truly, this food is being given to him who knows these two, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, as the eater of food and the giver of food;

he indeed becomes an eater of food, and food is surely bestowed upon him. The Full Moon sacrifice is the mind, for this mind is, as it were, full. The New Moon sacrifice is speech, for this speech is, as it were, visible.
Speech is this much with respect to the self; it is directly perceived as the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

When, on the day of preparation, he eats the food for undertaking the vow, by that he gratifies this much with respect to the self—directly perceived—as the New and Full Moon sacrifices; and by means of the sacrifice, he gratifies the two divine ones in the morning. 11.2.4 [8]

Regarding this they say: "Since no oblation is taken saying 'for the Full Moon,' nor is any oblation taken saying 'for the New Moon'; since one does not say 'recite for the Full Moon,' nor 'recite for the New Moon'; nor does one say 'sacrifice to the Full Moon,' nor 'sacrifice to the New Moon'—then by what means do his Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices become performed? That which he pours as an Āghāra-libation with the mind—for the mind, indeed, is [the essence].
By that [offering], he offers the Pūrṇamāsa; and as for the libation he pours upon Speech, Speech indeed is the Darśa—thereby he offers the Darśa.
Thus, his Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices become truly performed.
Now, some offer two *caru* oblations: one to Sarasvant on the full moon day, and one to Sarasvatī on the new moon day.

Some say, "We shall perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices as a direct perception [of these two]. One should not do so; for Sarasvant is indeed the mind and Sarasvatī is speech. When he pours out these two libations (āghāra), it is at that very moment that his New and Full Moon sacrifices become offered.
Therefore, one should not offer these two cooked rice oblations (caru). 11.2.4. [10]

Regarding this they say: "He who sacrifices with the New and Full Moon sacrifices becomes one who has made a formal resolve (*āgūrtin*). For having sacrificed with the Full Moon sacrifice, he knows, 'I shall sacrifice with the New Moon sacrifice'; and having sacrificed with the New Moon sacrifice, he knows, 'I shall sacrifice again with the Full Moon sacrifice. Thus, by means of his resolve alone, he goes to that world. When he goes to that world, how is it that he does not become one who has failed to resolve? It is when he [performs] these..."
In both cases he pours the two Āghāra libations; thus his New and Full Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsau) are completed.
When the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices have indeed been completed, he then goes to that world, and thus he becomes one who has not failed in his vow.
Now, even at this time they offer the Aśvamedha to the gods. Regarding this, they say: "The other [sacrifices] are merely the original form of the Aśvamedha."
Now, this very moon is indeed that Aśvamedha.

Regarding this, they say: "They offer an oblation at every step of the sacrificial horse. When one performs the Agnihotra sacrifice in the evening and the morning, one offers two oblations in the evening and two in the morning; these make four oblations. And the horse is four-footed; thus, it belongs to him.
At every single step, an oblation is offered.

Regarding this, they say: "One performs the sacrifice for the horse when it has turned back. King Soma is indeed the food of the gods, which is the moon. When, on that night, he is seen neither in the east nor in the west, then [one offers] this...
He comes to the world; he revolves in this world.

When he sacrifices with the new-moon offering (*amāvāsya*), he offers this sacrifice having already revolved. Then, when he sacrifices with the full-moon offering (*paurṇamāsa*), he immolates the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*); having immolated it, he presents it to the gods, or [at the end of] a year.
They immolate the other horse-sacrifice; for this month, revolving, makes up the year.
Thus, for him, the horse-sacrifice becomes immolated year after year.
Indeed, they immolate that very horse-sacrifice month after month. He who, knowing thus, [performs] the Agnihotra...
He offers oblations and sacrifices with the New and Full Moon sacrifices; indeed, month after month, his Aśvamedha sacrifice has been performed.
Thus, his Agnihotra and the New and Full Moon sacrifices become equivalent to the Aśvamedha.
The Praṇītā waters are indeed the head of the sacrifice. When he leads forth the Praṇītā waters, he thereby provides the head of the sacrifice.
"He who prepares it should know: 'This very thing is being prepared for me.

[11.2.6.2] "The vital breath (*prāṇa*) itself is its fuel, for by the vital breath all this is kindled—whatever breathes, whatever blinks, whatever moves. He should know: 'I myself am this fuel. [11.2.6.3]

The *sāmidhenī* verses follow his lineage; therefore, he should say to them, "Recite for me as if in continuous succession," for this lineage is indeed continuous. His mind and speech are the two *āghāra* libations—Sarasvant and Sarasvatī.
He should know: "My mind and speech are the two *āghāra* libations—Sarasvant and Sarasvatī. (11.2.6)

There are five fore-offerings (*prayāja*); these are his five vital breaths in the head. His first fore-offering is the mouth; the second is the right nostril; the third is the left nostril; the fourth is the right ear;
and the fifth is the left ear. Now, because he pours [the butter] together during the fourth fore-offering, therefore this hearing is internal.
The two eyes are the two *ājyabhāga* offerings; he should know, "These two are indeed my eyes.
Now, the cake (*puroḍāśa*) dedicated to Agni is his right side, and the *upāṃśuyāja* is his heart;
because they perform that [offering] in a whisper (*upāṃśu*), therefore this heart is as if hidden.

Now, that *puroḍāśa* offering to Agni and Soma is indeed its northern half; or the *sāṃnāyya* offering to Indra is its inner shoulder; the *sviṣṭakṛt* portion is its poison, and the *prāśitra* is [the remainder].
When he cuts off the *prāśitra*, it is just as that which was pierced from Prajāpati.
They cut away whatever was wrapped, whatever was knotted, and whatever was related to Varuṇa; even so they cut away this [part] of his.

He should know: "Just as they cut away that which was pierced from Prajāpati, so do they now cut away for me this which is wrapped, this which is knotted, and this which is related to Varuṇa. 11.2.6. [8]
The belly itself is his *iḍā*; just as they cut portions together for the *iḍā* here, even so this food of all forms is gathered together within the belly.
These three *anuyāja* offerings are his three downward breaths; his two arms are the *sūktavāka* and the [other] offering.

The *śamyorvāka* and the four *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings—these are the four supports; the two thighs and the two knees are the [other] two; and the *samiṣṭayajus* is his head. These are twenty-one oblations: the two *āghāra* libations, five *prayāja*s, two *ājyabhāga*s, and the offering to Agni.

The cake for Agni and Soma is tenfold: the Upāṃśuyāja for Agni and Soma, the cake for Agni and Soma, Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the Iḍā, three after-offerings (anuyājas), the Sūktavāka, and the Śamyorvāka; and furthermore, that which he takes up together during the Patnīsaṃyājas and the Samiṣṭayajus. 11.2.6. [11]

These are twenty-one oblations. There are twelve months in a year, five seasons, and three worlds—that makes twenty; and this one who shines yonder is the twenty-first. This is the goal, this is the foundation;
he thus goes to that goal, to that foundation. 11.2.6 [12]
Regarding this, Āruṇi said: "Indeed, fortnightly I become co-resident with that sun;
I know that perfection of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
Regarding this they say: "Is the self-sacrificer (ātmayājī) better, or the god-sacrificer (devayājī)? One should say, "The self-sacrificer. Now, he is indeed a self-sacrificer who...

"By this [mantra], this limb of mine is consecrated; by this, this limb of mine is restored. Just as a snake might cast off its skin, even so he is released from this mortal body, from evil. Consisting of the *Ṛg*, consisting of the *Yajuṣ*, consisting of the *Sāman*, and consisting of the oblation, he attains the heavenly world. 11.2.6. [14]

Now, he is indeed a sacrificer to the gods who knows: "I am sacrificing here to the gods alone; I am serving the gods. He is like one who brings tribute to a superior, or like a Vaiśya bringing tribute to a king; he does not win as great a world as the other does. 11.2.7. [1]
The year is the sacrifice. Whoever knows that "the year is the sacrifice," for him the sacrifice of this year is indeed performed at its end;
moreover, whatever is performed during the year—all that becomes attained, secured, and won by him. 11.2.7[2]
The seasons are the officiating priests. He who knows that "the seasons are the officiating priests" has his sacrifice among the seasons performed at the very end;

moreover, whatever is performed during the seasons, all of that becomes attained, secured, and won for him. The months are the oblations. He who knows that "the months are the oblations" has his sacrifice among the months performed at the very end.
Moreover, whatever is performed during the months, all that indeed becomes attained, secured, and conquered by him.
The half-months are the vessels for the oblations; he who knows that "the half-months are the vessels for the oblations" reaches the end.
Verily, his half-months become sacrificed; moreover, whatever is performed during the half-months, all that becomes attained, secured, and conquered by him.
Day and night are the two attendants; he who knows that day and night are the two attendants reaches the end.
Verily, his sacrifice is performed throughout day and night; moreover, whatever is done during day and night—all that becomes obtained, secured, and conquered by him.
This earth is the first *sāmidhenī*, Agni the second, Vāyu the third, and the atmosphere the fourth.

Heaven is the fifth, the sun the sixth, the moon the seventh, the mind the eighth, speech the ninth, austerity the tenth, and the Brahman the eleventh; for these indeed kindle all this, and by them all this is kindled; therefore they are called *sāmidhenīs*. 11.2.7. [7]
He indeed recites the first [verse] three times. When he recites it the first time, by that he conquers the eastern direction;
when he recites it the second time, by that he conquers the southern direction; when he recites it the third time, by that he conquers the upward direction.
He likewise recites the last [verse] three times. When he recites it the first time, by that he conquers the western direction.
With that which is the second [libation], he conquers the northern quarter; with that which is the third, he conquers this very foundation.
Thus indeed, by these [libations], he conquers these worlds and these quarters.
Truth is the first libation, reality is the latter; verily, he wins truth and reality, as well as whatever else there is.
"Everything is indeed conquerable through truth and sincerity; he conquers all that.
11.2.7.[10] "The first fore-offering is brilliance itself; the second is honor; the third is glory; the fourth is spiritual luster; the fifth is the eating of food. 11.2.7.[11]
He should consecrate the first fore-offering with "May I be full of splendor";
the second with "May I be full of honor"; the third with "May I be glorious"; the fourth with "May I be endowed with the luster of sacred knowledge";
and the fifth with "May I be an eater of food. Indeed, one becomes full of splendor, full of honor, glorious, endowed with the luster of sacred knowledge, and an eater of food.
He who knows this thus becomes so.

11.2.7.[12] Indeed, knowing this, Śvetaketu Āruṇeya used to say: "Who indeed would wish to see in future ages one who is like a great serpent coiled up, [thinking], 'He who knew thus the glory of the fore-sacrifices'? 11.2.7.[13]
The former butter-portion (ājyabhāga) is the past, and the latter is the future; verily, he wins both the past and the future.
Moreover, whatever is to be won by means of the past and the future, all that he indeed wins.
The cake (puroḍāśa) for Agni is the Brahman. He who knows that the cake for Agni is the Brahman, verily, he wins it.
He wins the Brahman, and whatever is to be won by the Brahman, all that he indeed wins.
The Upāṃśuyāja is the Kṣatra. He who knows that the Upāṃśuyāja is the Kṣatra wins the Kṣatra, and whatever is to be won by the Kṣatra, all that he indeed wins. Now, as for the Upāṃśuyāja—
Some perform it loudly, others in a whisper; therefore they declare it for the sake of the Kṣatra.
The cake (puroḍāśa) dedicated to Viśvedevas is the superior one. He who knows that "the cake dedicated to Viśvedevas is the superior one" indeed secures the people (viś);
moreover, whatever is to be won by the people, all that he wins. Now, as for the cake dedicated to Agni...
The *upāṃśuyāja* and the [first two *āghāra* offerings] come first; therefore both the priesthood (*brahman*) and the nobility (*kṣatra*) are established upon the peasantry (*viś*).
The *sāṃnāyya* offering is the kingdom. He who knows that the *sāṃnāyya* is the kingdom indeed secures the kingdom for himself;
moreover, whatever is to be won by means of the kingdom, all that he wins. Now, some prepare the *sāṃnāyya*.
From him many [beings] go forth; he gathers the kingdom together and disperses it.

11.2.7.[18] Austerity is the Sviṣṭakṛt. He who knows that "Austerity is the Sviṣṭakṛt" secures austerity for himself; moreover, whatever is to be won by austerity, all that he indeed wins. 11.2.7.[19]
The world is the *prāśitra*. He who knows that "the world is the *prāśitra*" indeed secures the world;

moreover, whatever is to be won by means of the world, all that he wins. He does not suffer harm from the world by a fragment (*lava*); for indeed, in yonder world, people suffer harm from the world by a fragment. But he who knows thus—even after having committed much evil—does not suffer harm from the world.

One trembles before the world. 11.2.7.[20] "Faith is the sacrificial ladle. He who knows that "faith is the sacrificial ladle" indeed secures faith; moreover, whatever is to be won through faith, all that he wins. 11.2.7.[21]
The first after-offering (anuyāja) is the thunderbolt; the second is the hailstone; the third is the firebrand.

11.2.7.[22] He should consecrate the first after-offering with the words, "O thunderbolt, strike so-and-so," naming whomsoever he hates; the second with, "O hailstone, strike so-and-so"; and the third with, "O firebrand, strike so-and-so. 11.2.7.[23]

He who dies suddenly—him the *anuyāja* called *aśani* strikes; then he who is like a flowing stream—him the *anuyāja* called *hrāduni* strikes; then he who is like a smoldering fire—him the *anuyāja* called *ulkūṣī* strikes. This is the *yajñamenī*. By means of this *menī*, the gods indeed caused the Asuras to perish; and so [it is for the sacrificer].
In this very way, a sacrificer who possesses such knowledge utterly destroys his evil, hateful rival.

If the sacrifice were to end with the after-offerings (*anuyāja*), it would end with thunderbolts, it would end with hailstones, or it would end with portents; therefore, the sacrifice of the gods ends either with the *iḍā* or with the *śamyu*.
By means of the *prayāja* offerings, the gods went to the heavenly world; the Asuras pursued them, but they repelled them with the *anuyāja* offerings.
Therefore, when the *anuyāja* offerings are performed, the sacrificer repels his evil, hateful rival. 11.2.7 [27]

The fore-offerings (prayāja) are indeed the out-breaths (prāṇa), and the after-offerings (anuyāja) are the in-breaths (apāna). Therefore, the fore-offerings are offered facing forward, for that is the form of the out-breath; the after-offerings face backward, for that is the form of the in-breath. These, indeed, are the Upasad rites of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
Because they are the after-offerings (*anuyāja*), therefore they are offered facing westward in the form of the *upasad*s.
11.2.7.[28] The *sūktavāka* is the conclusion (*saṃsthā*). Verily, he who knows that the *sūktavāka* is the conclusion secures the conclusion;
moreover, whatever is to be won by the conclusion, all that he wins, and he reaches the end of his life. 11.2.7.[29]
The *śamyorvāk* is the foundation. He who knows that "the *śamyorvāk* is the foundation" indeed secures a foundation for himself;
moreover, whatever is to be won by means of a foundation, all that he wins and attains a firm foundation.
Those gods performed these *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings on the west side; they thereby placed a pair [of male and female] upon the rear.

It is for the sake of procreation that the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings are made; thus he places a productive pair behind him for the sake of procreation. Verily, one is born after the procreation of the gods; he who knows this is born through every pair. 11.2.7 [31]
Food is the *samiṣṭayajus*. He who knows that food is the *samiṣṭayajus* indeed secures food for himself;
moreover, whatever is to be won by means of food, all that he wins. 11.2.7 [32] The year is the sacrificer; the seasons officiate for him as priests. Spring is the *āgnīdhra*; therefore, in spring...
The forest fires roam about; for that is the form of Agni. Summer is the Adhvaryu;

summer is indeed as if heated, and the Adhvaryu goes forth as if heated. The rainy season is the Udgātṛ; therefore, when it rains heavily, it is like the rhythmic beating of a *sāman*. Autumn is the Brahman; therefore, when the grain ripens, there are [offerings] accompanied by the *brahman*.
"Offspring," they say, is the winter; therefore, when the *vaṣaṭ* call is made in winter, cattle perish. Indeed, these deities officiate as priests for him.
If those who are not masters of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice were to officiate for him, he should meditate upon these very deities in his mind;
then these deities indeed officiate as priests for him. 11.2.7 [33]
Now, this very southern edge of the altar is the scale. Whatever one does that is good, that is within the altar;

and whatever one does that is not good, that is outside the altar. Therefore, one should sit as if touching the southern edge of the altar. For they place [the goods] on the scale in yonder world, and it will follow whichever side it tips toward—whether it be the good or the not-good. And he who...

Thus, indeed, he ascends the scales in this very world; in the other world, he is established upon the scales and is released from his good deeds, for they do not weigh him down, nor do his evil deeds. 11.3.1.
Speech, indeed, is the Agnihotra-cow of this Agnihotra, and the mind is the calf. Thus, this mind and speech—
Being indeed the same, they are yet distinct; therefore, by means of the common rope, people designate both the calf and the mother.
Radiance itself is faith, and truth is the clarified butter. 11.3.1.
[2] Janaka of Videha then asked Yājñavalkya: "Do you know the Agnihotra, Yājñavalkya?"
"O Samrāj, what is the Veda? "It is milk alone.
"If there were no milk, with what would one sacrifice? "With rice and barley. "If there were no rice and barley, with what would one sacrifice?
"With whatever other herbs there are. "If there were no other herbs, with what would one sacrifice? "With those that grow in the forest."

"If there were no herbs, with what would one sacrifice? With the products of trees. "If there were no water, with what would one sacrifice? He said: "At that time, indeed, nothing at all existed here; yet this was sacrificed as truth within faith."
"Do you know the Agnihotra, Yājñavalkya? I will give you a hundred cows," he said.

Regarding this, there are these verses: "What does the knower of the Agnihotra do when he departs from his home? How is his wisdom maintained? How is he continuously connected with the fires? How is it that his [sacrifice] remains as if he has not gone away?"—this is what he asks by saying this.

"He who is the swiftest among beings—he, the wise one, knows [this] even while traveling abroad; such is his poetic power, such is his continuity through the fires"—by this he speaks of the mind; for by the mind alone it remains unabsent from him. (11.3.1) "When he has gone far away and then becomes heedless there, in what place is that oblation of his offered which belongs to him at home?"

"When one offers oblations," he says, "and having gone far away, then becomes negligent there—in whom, then, is his oblation offered? This is what he means to say. (11.3.1) "He who is awake among the worlds, who has sustained all created beings—in him is that oblation of his offered, which belongs to his house. (11.3.2)
"He offers"—this he says regarding the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Therefore they say: "The *agnihotra* is indeed the vital breath.

Now, whoever knows the six pairs in the *agnihotra*, he is procreated through every form of generation, pair by pair—both the sacrificer and his wife. That constitutes one pair; therefore, his *agnihotra* is accompanied by a wife.

Thinking, "May I obtain this pair," there is the calf and the *agnihotra* cow—this is one pair; therefore, his *agnihotra* cow should have a male calf, thinking, "May I obtain this pair. There is the cooking pot and the embers—this is one pair;
the large offering-spoon (*sruk*) and the small offering-spoon (*sruva*)—this is one pair; the *āhavanīya* fire and the fuel-stick (*samidh*)—this is one pair.

The pair consists of the oblation and the utterance *svāhā*; this is one pair. Indeed, there are these six pairs in the Agnihotra. He who knows this is procreated through each of these pairs, by means of all forms of progeny. 11.3.3. [1]
Brahman indeed delivered the creatures to Death; he did not, however, deliver the religious student (*brahmacārin*) to him.
He [Death] said, "Let there be for me also a share in this. [Brahman replied], "On whatever night the student does not bring firewood.
Therefore, on whichever night a religious student does not bring firewood, he dwells having taken away a portion of his own life-span.

"Therefore, a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) should fetch fuel, lest he dwell having cut off a portion of his life. (11.3.3) "He who enters upon the life of a student of sacred knowledge indeed enters upon a long sacrificial session (*dīrghasattra*).

The fuel-stick (*samidh*) which he places on the fire when entering [the vow] is the introductory offering (*prāyaṇīyā*); that which he places when about to bathe [at the conclusion] is the concluding offering (*udayanīyā*); and those which are between these two—"
When a Brāhmaṇa, entering upon the life of a student (*brahmacarya*), enters those very quarters of him;
he enters the beings in four parts: one quarter into fire, one quarter into death, and one quarter into the teacher; thus, his fourth quarter remains in himself alone.
When he brings fuel for Agni, he thereby ransoms that very foot of his which is in Agni; having consecrated it, he places it within himself, and it enters him.
(11.3.3) Now, when he begs as one who has made himself poor, being without shame, he [ransoms] that very [foot] of his which is in Death.
That which is his foot, he ransoms with that; having consecrated it, he places it within himself, and it enters him.

11.3.3.[6] Now, when he obeys the word of the teacher and performs service for the teacher—that which is his foot belonging to the teacher—he ransoms with that; having consecrated it, he places it within himself, and it enters him. 11.3.3.[7]

"One should certainly not beg after having bathed; for by bathing, one conquers the begging of alms, the hunger of kinsmen, and the hunger of ancestors. One who knows this should beg from whichever woman he considers most praiseworthy—so they say, 'That is conducive to the world. Even if he does not find another woman from whom to beg, [he may still do so]."

He should beg from his own teacher’s wife, or else from his own mother; he should not pass the seventh [house] without having begged. All the Vedas enter him who knows this and practices in this manner.
Just as a kindled fire shines, even so does he shine after his bath who, knowing this, practices the life of a student.

He practiced [the rite]. 11.4.1.[1] Uddālaka Āruṇi, having been chosen by those from the North, caused them to run [in a chariot race]. A gold coin (*niṣka*) had been placed upon him; for indeed, among the ancient ones who were chosen and caused to run, a single prize (*ekadhana*) was placed there as a wager.

Fear came upon those northern Brāhmaṇas as they were afraid. "This is a Brāhmaṇa from Kuru-Pañcāla, a son of a Brāhmaṇa. If he does not yield half [of our territory] to us, come, let us challenge him to a theological debate (brahmodya). "By what hero? "By Svaidāyana," said Śaunaka.

There was Svaidāyana (Śvaidāyana). They said, "Svaidāyana, let us fight this man with you as our hero. He replied, "Stay here for now; let me first find out about him. He approached him, and as he had approached, [the other] spoke to him.
"O Svaidāyana! "Ho! O son of Gautama! the other replied. He then resolved to question him right there.
"O son of Gautama, he indeed would drive the people away who knows the eight [verses] of the New and Full Moon sacrifices."
One should know five *ājyabhāga* offerings before [the principal oblations], six *havirbhāga* offerings in the middle, and eight *prājāpatya* offerings and eight *ājyabhāga* offerings after.
O son of Gautama, one who has been chosen should cause the people to run.
He who knows this regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices— that from which these offspring are born toothless, from which they are born [with teeth],
from which their [teeth] fall out, from which they remain steady,
from which in the final stage of life all of them fall out again, and from which the lower ones are born first and then the upper ones— [attains the fruit thereof].
Because those below are indeed finer, while those above are broader; because the tusks are longer, and the canine teeth are equal.
O son of Gautama, let him who is thus chosen drive the people.

He who would know this regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices: why these offspring are born with hair; why for them the beards, the armpit-hair, and the body-hair grow again as it were; and why one first becomes grey only on the head, but later in the final stage of life, everyone becomes grey all over. 11.4.1 [7]
O son of Gautama, he who knows this regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices may indeed cause the people to run about; for he knows why the semen of a boy, once emitted, does not come to fruition,
why it comes to fruition in his middle age, and why it no longer does so in his final age.
"It is possible that one might know the golden Gāyatrī, whose wings are light, who carries the sacrificer to the heavenly world.
To him he gave a gold necklace, saying, "You are a learned man, O Svaidāyana; indeed, they give gold to one who knows gold."
Having embraced him, he went out. They asked him: "What was this Gautama’s son like? He said: "He was like Brahmā, the son of Brahmā; his head would have burst asunder had anyone reviled him.
Thereupon they departed from that very place. Then, carrying fuel in his hands, he returned to him, saying: "I wish to become your pupil."
"What is it that you wish to be instructed in? Tell me those very questions which you asked me.
He replied, "I shall tell them to you even though you have not yet been initiated.
He then said this to him: "There are two *āghāra* libations, five *prayāja* offerings, and the *ājyabhāga* for Agni as the eighth; these are the eight."
The *ājyabhāga* offerings come first; the *saumya-ājyabhāga* is the first among the portions of the oblations, for Soma is indeed an oblation.
The *puroḍāśa* for Agni, the *upāṃśuyāja* for Agni-Soma, and the *puroḍāśa* for Agni-Soma, as well as Agni Sviṣṭakṛt—these five are the portions of the oblations in the middle. 11.4.1 [11]

The *prāśitra*, the *iḍā*, that which he places for the *āgnīdhra*, the portion for the *brahmán*, the portion for the sacrificer, and the *anvāhārya*—these six belong to Prajāpati; the three *anuyāja*s, the four *patnīsaṃyāja*s, and the *samiṣṭayajus* as the eighth—these eight are the subsequent *ājyabhāga*s. 11.4.1. [12]
Now, because the fore-offerings (*prayāja*) are without invitatory formulas (*puro'nuvākyā*), therefore these creatures are born toothless;

and because the oblations (*havīṃṣi*) have invitatory formulas, therefore their teeth grow; and because the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) are without invitatory formulas, therefore their teeth fall out; and because the offerings to the wives (*patnīsaṃyāja*) have invitatory formulas.

Therefore, they remain united; and because the *samiṣṭayajus* offering is performed without a preceding *anuvākyā*, therefore in their final stage of life, all of them become completely separated. Then, because one sacrifices with the *yājyā* after having recited the *anuvākyā*, therefore the lower ones are born first, and then the upper ones.

Because one sacrifices with a *triṣṭubh* after reciting a *gāyatrī*, therefore the lower [teeth] are smaller and the upper ones are broader; and because he pours the two libations forward, therefore the upper fangs are longer; and because the two *saṃyājyā* verses are indeed in the same metre, therefore the rows of teeth are equal. 11.4.1. [14]

Now, because he spreads the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), therefore these creatures are born with hair; and because he spreads the *prastara* as it were again, therefore their beards, armpit hair, and body hair grow back again;
and because he throws the *prastara* into the fire first by itself alone, therefore one becomes grey first on the head. And then...
Because he throws all the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) into the fire at once, therefore, in the final stage of life, everyone becomes entirely grey.
Now, because the *prayāja* offerings consist of clarified butter (*ājya*) as the oblation, therefore the seed emitted by a youth does not coagulate;
it remains like water, for clarified butter is indeed like water. Then, that which occurs in the middle of the sacrifice...
They sacrifice with curds and a cake; therefore, he is capable of procreation in his middle age, for he is like a drop, and seed is indeed like a drop.
And because the after-offerings consist of ghee as the oblation, therefore he is not capable of procreation again in his final age; he is like water, for ghee is indeed like water. 11.4.1 [16]
The altar itself is the Gāyatrī. Those eight butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) which are in front are its right wing;
those eight butter-portions which are behind are its left wing. This very Gāyatrī, tawny-hued and having light for wings, carries the sacrificer who knows this thus to the heavenly world. 11.4.2. [1]

Now, therefore, regarding the taking up of the two offering-spoons (*sruc*): some who consider themselves experts take up the *juhū* with the right hand and the *upabhṛt* with the left. One should not do it thus; for if someone were to say of him then, "This Adhvaryu has made the sacrificer's hateful rival a match for him, one who rises against him," he would indeed be liable [to that fate].

It should be exactly so. 11.4.2.[2] One should act precisely in this manner: grasping the *juhū* with both hands, one should place it upon the *upabhṛt*; there is no deliberation regarding that; it is conducive to cattle and conducive to long life for you.
He should take it up without clinking it together; for if he were to clink it together, insecurity would befall the sacrificer.
Therefore, he should take it up without clinking it together.
Now, therefore, concerning the stepping across: one Adhvaryu, indeed, by means of the thunderbolt, scatters the sacrificer's cattle; [he does so] with the thunderbolt.

"Alas! Another is piling it up against him. Indeed, that Adhvaryu smites the sacrificer's cattle with the thunderbolt when he steps across with his right foot while about to call for the *śrauṣaṭ*, and then calls for the *śrauṣaṭ* with his left. But this one piles it up against him; he who, being about to call for the *śrauṣaṭ*, steps across with his left foot and then calls for the *śrauṣaṭ* with his right—this one indeed piles it up against him. 11.4.2. [4]

Now, concerning the holding [of the ladles]: some who consider themselves experts hold up their arms and maintain the two offering-ladles (*srucau*) in that manner. One should not do so; for if someone were to say of him then, "This Adhvaryu has indeed made his arms into spears; he will become one with spear-like arms," it would likely come to pass exactly so. Now, this is the middle vital breath (*prāṇa*); therefore, [one should hold them] from there.
One should hold it up and set it down in that very manner.

Now, therefore, concerning the *āśrāvaṇa* (the call for attention): there are six ways of sounding the *āśrāvaṇa*—downward, horizontal, upward, wretchedly, with external splendor, and with internal splendor.
Indeed, this is the downward way: when one takes something up loudly and sets it down quietly; if one should desire of someone, "May he become worse off," [then one should do so].
Taking it up high, he should set it down slowly; by that, he becomes worse.

Now, this is the horizontal method: with exactly as much [wood] as he takes up, he sets it down. If he should desire, "May he be neither better nor worse," then with exactly as much as he takes up, he should set it down; by that, he is neither...
"He becomes better, not worse.
11.4.2.[8] Now, this is the case for one who, having taken something up slowly, places it down loudly; if he should desire, "May he become better," then for him—
Taking it up slowly, he should place it high; by that, he becomes superior.
Now, this is pitiable: when one makes the announcement in a low, long-drawn, and toneless manner.
If someone were to say of him then, "This Adhvaryu has indeed made the sacrificer pitiable before his enemies," [it would be so].

"One who [addresses him] as 'the one who lies in wait for his kinsman' would surely become so himself. (11.4.2.10) "Now, this is the one devoid of external splendor: when he calls for the *āśrāvaṇa* loudly with his lips apart and without a tone, splendor is indeed the tone;
thus he places splendor outside himself and becomes hungry. (11.4.2.11)
Now, this is the one who possesses internal splendor (*antaḥśrī*): when he has joined his lips together, he causes the announcement to be made loudly with a resonant tone (*svaravat*).
Splendor, indeed, is the resonant tone; thus he places splendor within himself and becomes an eater of food.
He should place it, as it were, softly in the chest, then strike out on both sides, and finally settle it loudly at the end in the *bārhata* manner. Of that—

There is no comparison; that [offering] is conducive to cattle and long life. 11.4.2. Now, therefore, regarding the *homā* (oblation): some who consider themselves experts, having brought down the *sruc* spoon toward the east, having offered, and having carried it around, place it upon the *upabhṛt* spoon.
One should not do so; for if someone were to say of him in that case, "Verily, you have made it subject to the *anuyāja*s..."
"This Adhvaryu has brought down the sacrificer to the level of his hateful rival who dwells alongside him"—thus [the rival] would indeed be liable to prevail.
Some, having lowered the *sruk* from the side, having offered the oblation, and having carried it around, place it upon the *upabhṛt*; one should not do so.
If someone were to do this, one should say of him: "This Adhvaryu has offered the oblations through a non-designated opening;
he will either perish or become worm-eaten. Indeed, it would be likely to happen exactly so.
One should rather act in this way: having drawn down the ladle toward the east and having made the offering...
Having taken [the butter] from that very [pot], he should place it into the *upabhṛt* vessel; there is no need for deliberation regarding this, for it is beneficial for cattle and promotes longevity.

11.4.2. [16] One kind of Adhvaryu, indeed, burns the oblations, while another satisfies the oblations. That Adhvaryu who, having offered the clarified butter (*ājya*), offers the portions (*avadāna*) is one who burns the oblations; this one, indeed—

Then an unseen voice spoke: "This Adhvaryu has indeed consumed his oblations by burning them up! But he truly satisfies them who, having offered the clarified butter, offers the portions of the victim, and finally offers again with clarified butter; he is the one who satisfies them. When they are satisfied, the gods fill for him golden cups. 11.4.2 [17]

Regarding this, Yājñavalkya said: "In that one spreads an underlayer [of ghee], takes a portion, and pours ghee over it, by that very act one satisfies them; when they are satisfied, the gods fill their golden cups for those whose householder is Ayasthūṇa. Now, Śaulbāyana was the Adhvaryu priest for those whose householder was Ayasthūṇa. 11.4.2. [18]

He said: "This sacrificial session here has lean cattle and little clarified butter, and yet this householder thinks, 'I am [the performer]'? He said: "O Adhvaryu, you have not cried out for us; these indeed are your two offering-spoons which you were unable to take up for a year.
If I were to instruct you in these two, you would surely multiply with offspring and cattle and attain the heavenly world."

"Carry [the sacrifice] to the world," [he said]. 11.4.2.[20] He (Yājñavalkya) said, "I shall come to you as a pupil. He (Janaka) said, "Indeed, you are worthy of this very thing, since you have been our Adhvaryu for a year; I shall tell this to you even though you have not yet approached me as a pupil. And he told that very same thing to him.

Regarding the taking up of the two offering-spoons (*sruc*), he spoke this explanation; therefore, one should appoint as *adhvaryu* priest only one who knows thus, and not one who does not know thus. 11.4.3.
Prajāpati, while creating living beings, performed austerity. From him, being exhausted by that austerity, Śrī (Prosperity) departed. She...
Blazing, radiant, and flickering, she stood there; the gods meditated upon her as she was blazing, radiant, and flickering. 11.4.3[2]

They said to Prajāpati, "Let us kill her; let us take this [portion] from her. He said, "This Śrī is indeed a woman, and one does not kill a woman; moreover, you shall take it from her while she is still alive.
Agni took from her food; Soma, the king, took sovereignty; Varuṇa took imperial rule; Mitra took the power of the nobility; Indra took strength.
Bṛhaspati [gave] strength, Savitṛ spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), Pūṣan the kingdom, Sarasvatī fortune, Tvaṣṭṛ nourishment, and Puṣṭi forms.
She said to Prajāpati, "He has indeed consumed this of mine. He said, "Ask them for it back by means of a sacrifice."
He saw this sacrifice consisting of ten oblations: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma,
a cake on ten potsherds for Varuṇa, a pap for Mitra, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra,
a pap for Bṛhaspati, and a cake on twelve potsherds or eight potsherds for Savitṛ.
A pap for Pūṣan, a pap for Sarasvatī, and a cake on ten potsherds for Tvaṣṭṛ.

He addressed these with this invitatory verse: "May Agni, Soma, Varuṇa, Mitra, Indra, Bṛhaspati, Savitṛ who is thousandfold, Pūṣan with his cattle, Sarasvatī with her protection, and Tvaṣṭṛ anoint our forms with sacrifices. These [are the deities].
They stood facing him.
He approached them from the further side in reverse order with this *yājyā* verse: "May Sarasvatī, bestowing forms, Pūṣan, Bhaga, and Savitṛ grant to me;
may Bṛhaspati grant, and Indra strength to me; may Mitra [grant] sovereignty and Varuṇa [grant] dominion."
"Let Soma be the fire," they resolved, intending to give it back again.
11.4.3.[8] She saw these secondary oblations (*upahoma*): "May Agni, the eater of food, the lord of food, bestow the eating of food upon me at this sacrifice—*svāhā*!
Having taken up the oblation itself, Agni went forth; he gave the eating of food back to her once more. 11.4.3.[9]
"May Soma, the king, the lord of kings, bestow sovereignty upon me in this sacrifice—svāhā! Having taken the oblation, Soma departed; he bestowed sovereignty back upon her.
"May Varuṇa, the sovereign, the lord of sovereigns, bestow sovereignty upon me in this sacrifice."
Saying "Svāhā!", Varuṇa took the oblation and departed; he restored sovereign rule to her once again. 11.4.3.
