[11] "May Mitra, the lord of the kṣatra, bestow the kṣatra upon me in this sacrifice, svāhā!"—saying this, Mitra took the oblation.
Indra departed; he gave back the *kṣatra* (sovereignty) to her.
"May Indra, the lord of strength, bestow strength upon me in this sacrifice, svāhā!"—taking the oblation itself, Indra departed and gave back the strength to her.

"Bṛhaspati is the sacred formulation; may Bṛhaspati bestow upon me at this sacrifice the splendor of sacred formulation, svāhā!"—taking the oblation itself, Bṛhaspati ascended and bestowed the splendor of sacred formulation back upon her.
"Savitṛ is the kingdom, the lord of the kingdom; may Savitṛ bestow upon me at this sacrifice the kingdom, svāhā!"—taking the oblation itself...
Savitṛ stepped forth; he restored the kingdom to her.
"May Pūṣan, the lord of fortune, bestow fortune upon me at this sacrifice—svāhā! Having taken up the oblation, Pūṣan stepped forth; he restored fortune to her. 11.4.3 [15–16]
"May Sarasvatī, the mistress of nourishment, bestow nourishment upon me at this sacrifice—Svāhā! Having taken the oblation, Sarasvatī departed; she bestowed nourishment back upon her.
"Tvaṣṭṛ, the maker of forms and the lord of forms, shall bestow cattle with their forms upon me at this sacrifice."

Saying "Svāhā!", Tvaṣṭṛ took the oblation itself and departed; he restored the cattle to her by means of their form. Ten are the sacrificial gifts; ten-by-ten is the Virāj; the Virāj is prosperity; indeed, ten-by-ten are the sacrificial gifts; ten-by-ten is the Virāj; the Virāj is prosperity; [one attains] prosperity through the Virāj. 11.4.3. [18]

These indeed are ten deities, ten oblations, and ten offerings; thus he becomes established in the Virāj, which consists of food. For this [sacrifice], there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses; he sacrifices to the deities in a whisper; there are five *prayāja*s, three *anuyāja*s, and one *samiṣṭayajus*; the two *ājyabhāga*s are characterized by prosperity through Agni.

"May he obtain wealth and nourishment day by day, glorious and most rich in heroes; may Soma be our good friend—he who increases the household, drives away disease, finds treasure, and augments prosperity. Let these two *saṃyājyā* verses contain the word "thousand":
"Now grant us, O Agni, thousandfold wealth, accompanied by offspring and nourishment, resplendent and full of heroic power."

"The most excellent, unfailing one; and do thou, O Brahman, who art best invoked by the gods, protect us in our hymns. Shine auspiciously for us, O Agni, strengthened by the Maruts, the greatest winner of thousands! 11.4.3. [20] Gotama Rāhūgaṇa discovered this very [verse]; it indeed brought him face to face with Janaka of Videha. It—[he recited].

He searched for her among the Hāṅgija Brāhmaṇas, and he found her with Yājñavalkya. He said, "O Yājñavalkya, I give you a thousand [cows], since we have found Mitravindā in you. One who, knowing this, performs this sacrifice, finds a friend; his kingdom prospers, he conquers rebirth, and he reaches a full lifespan.

He who knows this thus also sacrifices. 11.4.4.[1] Now, therefore, follows the prosperity of the oblation. There are indeed six doors of Brahman: fire, wind, water, the moon, lightning, and the sun. 11.4.4.[2]
He who sacrifices with an offering that has been scorched enters through Agni as the door of Brahman;
having entered through Agni as the door of Brahman, he wins union with Brahman and residence in the same world as Brahman.
Now, he who sacrifices with an offering that has fallen down enters through Vāyu as the door of Brahman; he...

By means of the wind, having entered through the door of Brahman, he attains union with Brahman and the same world as Brahman. 11.4.4[4] Now, he who sacrifices with uncooked oblations enters through the door of Brahman by means of water;
he enters through the door of Brahman by means of water. 11.4.4[5]
Now, he who sacrifices with an oblation that is reddened enters through the door of Brahman by means of the moon;
he, having entered through the door of Brahman by means of the moon— 11.4.4 [6]—and he who sacrifices with a bloody oblation enters through the door of Brahman by means of lightning; he...
By means of lightning, one enters through the door of Brahman. Now, he who sacrifices with well-cooked oblations enters through the door of Brahman by means of Āditya;
having entered through the door of Brahman by means of Āditya, he wins union with Brahman and residence in the same world as Brahman. This is that.
This is the perfection of the oblation. Indeed, for one who knows this perfection of the oblation in this way, his sacrifice becomes performed with a completely perfect oblation.
11.4.4. Now, therefore, follows the perfection of the sacrifice. Whatever is deficient in the sacrifice, that is its means of procreation. And so...
That which is redundant in his sacrifice is for cattle; that which is superfluous is for prosperity; and that which is complete is for the heavenly world.
If he should think, "Something deficient has occurred in my sacrifice," let him know: "This is productive for me; I shall procreate. 11.4.4 [9]
One should meditate upon that.
11.4.4.[10] Now, if one should think, "Something has been redundant in my sacrifice," he should meditate upon it thus: "This is beneficial for cattle; I shall become possessed of cattle. 11.4.4.[11]

Now, if he should think, "My sacrifice has become precarious," let him meditate on this [offering], thinking: "This [offering] of mine will go to Prosperity (Śrī), surrounded by splendor, fame, and the luster of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcasa). 11.4.4. Then, if he should think, "My sacrifice has been successful," let him meditate on this [offering], thinking: "This [offering] of mine is conducive to heaven; it is the heavenly world. 11.4.5.

"One should worship it with the thought, 'I shall come into being. This is the perfection of the sacrifice. Indeed, for one who knows this perfection of the sacrifice in this way, his sacrifice becomes offered with all perfections. Urvaśī, the Apsaras, desired Purūravas, the son of Iḍā. Having found him, she said to him: "Three times a day..."
"Do not lie down with me when I am unwilling, struck as I am by a cane-staff; do not let me see you naked.
This indeed is not the proper conduct for women.
She lived with him for a long time, and she even became pregnant by him; she lived with him for a very long time, and then—

The Gandharvas deliberated: "For a long time indeed this Urvaśī has dwelt among mortals; devise a means by which she might come back. Two rams were tied to her bed; then the Gandharvas released one of the rams. 11.5.1 [3]
She said, "Alas, they are carrying away my son like one who has no hero, like one who has no kinsman! A second time they carried him off, and she spoke exactly as before.
Then he reflected: "How indeed could that place be without a hero, how could it be without a kinsman, where I myself am? He...

He sprang up naked; he thought for a long time that he would put on his garment. Then the Gandharvas produced lightning, and they saw him naked as if by day. Thereupon she vanished, thinking, "I am going back.
While muttering to himself, "She has vanished," he wandered through Kurukṣetra toward the Plakṣa tree known as Anyataḥplakṣa.
Bisavatī went toward her with a loud cry; then those Apsarases, having become birds, flew all around her.
Knowing this, she said, "This is indeed that man with whom I dwelt. They said, "Let us reveal ourselves to him," and saying, "So be it," they revealed themselves to him.

Having recognized her, he addressed her: "O wife, stay here in your mind, O fierce one! Let us now exchange words together; these unspoken mantras of ours shall bring us joy even on the further day. "Come, let us rest; let us speak together"—this is what he said to her. 11.5.1 [7]
She replied to him: "What shall I do with these words of yours? I have already departed like the first light of dawn;
go back to your home, Purūravas! I am as difficult to capture as the wind. He said: "You did not do what I told you; indeed, I am now difficult for you to reach. Go back to your home!"

He indeed said this to him: 11.5.1. Then this dejected man said: "May the fortunate one fly away today, never to return; may he go to the furthest distance, and then lie in the lap of Destruction, and may the impetuous wolves devour him. Thus spoke the fortunate one today.
"Bind it, or else it will fly away; then wolves or dogs might devour it"—this is what she said.
Then the other replied to him: "Purūravas, do not die! Do not fly away! Let not malevolent wolves devour you!
There are no friendships with women; these are but the hearts of hyenas. Do not take this to heart. Indeed, it is not so.
"Friendship with women is [transient]; come back to the house," he said to him.

"Since I, O Virūpa, wandered among mortals and dwelt there for four autumns, eating a single drop of ghee once a day—it is by that alone that I now wander, fully satisfied. This is the dialogue consisting of fifteen verses which the Bahvṛcas recite.
They said to him, "He has indeed pierced his heart.

She said, "Come on the night of the year's end; you shall lie with me for one night at the end, and then this son of yours will be born. He came on the night of the year's end to the golden pavilions.
Then they said to him alone, "Enter this. So they led her forward to him.
She said, "The Gandharvas will indeed give you a boon tomorrow morning; choose it from them. He said, "You yourself must choose it for me.
She said, "Tell them, 'May I be one of you alone. And so, in the morning, the Gandharvas gave him the boon.
He said, "May I be one of you alone.

They said, "Indeed, among humans there is no sacrificial body of Agni by which, having sacrificed with it, you might become one of us. They poured fire into a cooking pot and gave it to him, saying, "Having sacrificed with this, you shall become one of us. And so they gave it to him.

Taking the boy with him, he went away; having deposited the fire in the forest, he returned to the village with the boy alone, saying, "I am coming back. That fire which had vanished entered the *aśvattha* tree, and that sacrificial pot entered the *śamī* tree.
He then went again to the Gandharvas. 11.5.1. [14]

They said, "Cook for a year rice fit for the four priests to eat; then, having anointed three kindling-sticks each from this very *aśvattha* tree with ghee, he should place them on the fire with verses containing the word 'kindling-stick' (*samidh*) and the word 'ghee' (*ghṛta*).
That fire which is produced therefrom shall indeed become that [fire]. 11.5.1. [15]

They said, "This is as if indirect; rather, make the upper fire-drill (*uttarāraṇi*) of *aśvattha* wood and the lower fire-drill (*adharāraṇi*) of *śamī* wood. Whatever fire is produced from that shall be that very [fire]. They said, "This is as if indirect; rather, make the upper fire-drill of *aśvattha* wood and the lower fire-drill of *aśvattha* wood."
"That fire which was produced from that [wood] shall indeed become that very same one. 11.5.1.
[17] He made the upper fire-drill (*araṇi*) of *aśvattha* wood and the lower fire-drill of *aśvattha* wood. That fire which was born from that became that very same one.
Having sacrificed with it, he became one of the Gandharvas. Therefore, the upper fire-drill should be of *aśvattha* wood.

One should make the lower fire-drill from the wood of the *aśvattha* tree; the fire that is produced therefrom is indeed that very [fire]. Having sacrificed with it, one becomes one of the Gandharvas.
11.5.2. Prajāpati, indeed, fashioned himself by means of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices; he [fashioned] this very right arm.
He prepared the Vaiśvadeva oblation; of that [oblation], this very thumb is the oblation for Agni, this is for Soma, this is for Savitṛ.
That cake (puroḍāśa) is indeed the largest; therefore, among these [fingers], this one is the largest. This is for Sarasvatī.
Now, that which is above the hand is for Pūṣan; that which is the joint [of the arm] is for the Maruts; this forearm is for the Viśvedevas;
and that which is the upper arm is for Heaven and Earth. That [portion] is indeed undefined (anirukta); therefore it is undefined.
This very right thigh is the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings; those five oblations belonging to it are these [fingers].
The five fingers and the two ankles are for Indra and Agni; that oblation belongs to two deities, therefore these two ankles are here.
This [part] is for Varuṇa, this for the Maruts, and the spine is for Ka; that indeed is undefined, therefore it is undefined. 11.5.2. [4]
The Anīkavatī sacrifice is his mouth, for the mouth is the army (*anīka*) of the vital breaths. The Sāṃtapanīya sacrifice is his chest, for with the chest one is heated all over.
The Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice is his belly; the belly is indeed a foundation, and it serves for the sake of stability.
The Kraiḍina oblation is his sexual organs, for with the sexual organs one plays, as it were. This downward breath is the Āditya sacrifice. 11.5.2 [5]

This very upper thigh is Mahāhavis. Those five oblations of his which are combined together are these five toes. The Aindrāgna oblation is the two ankles; for that belongs to two deities, therefore there are these two ankles.
This [other part] is the Māhendra, and this is the Vaiśvakarmana; for that indeed is undefined.

Therefore, that [offering] is undefined (*anirukta*). Now, that which is here within the belly—that is the sacrifice to the Fathers (*pitṛyajña*); and that indeed is undefined, therefore it is undefined. 11.5.2.
This very left arm is the *Śunāsīrīya*; those five oblations of it which are common to all are these [fingers].

Then, these five fingers and that joint of the hand which is above are the *tvaṣṭṛ* [portion]; this [forearm] is the *vāyavya*, and that [upper arm] is the *saurya*. Now, that [upper arm] is undefined; therefore it is undefined. These Cāturmāsya sacrifices have three joints and two parts joined together; therefore, these are the limbs of a person.
The threefold sets are doubled; for those four [sacrifices], there are three-three undefined oblations for two of them, and two-two for the other two.
For those four, they churn the fire; therefore, it is brought with four limbs, and they lead it forward for two of them.
Therefore, by means of these two [seasons], thus indeed did Prajāpati fashion himself through the Cāturmāsyas;
and in the same way, the sacrificer who knows this fashions himself through the Cāturmāsyas.
Regarding this they say: "The Vaiśvadeva oblation should be entirely in the *gāyatrī* metre, and the Varuṇapraghāsas should be entirely in the *triṣṭubh* metre."
"The entire world is the great oblation; the Śunāsīrīya sacrifice consists entirely of *anuṣṭubh* verses for the sake of attaining the fourfold *stoma*.
One should not do it in that way; rather, by the very fact that these [verses] amount to those [required], his desire is thereby attained.
These Cāturmāsya sacrifices, indeed, amount to three hundred and sixty-two *bṛhatī* verses; thus, by means of these...

He obtains both the year-long vow and the great vow; moreover, this sacrificer is indeed established on two feet, and thus he causes the sacrificer himself to attain and be firmly established in the heavenly world.
Śauceya Prācīnayogya went to Uddālaka Āruṇi for a theological debate concerning the Agnihotra.
"I desire to know," [he said].

He (the king) replied, "Gautama, what is your *agnihotrī* cow? What is her calf? What is the one brought near her? What is the joining? What is being milked? What is the milk? What is being brought forth? What is placed on the fire? What is being illuminated?"
What was brought back by the waters? What was being removed? What was removed?

What was being lifted up? What was lifted up? What was raised? What was being carried away? What was restrained? Which fuel-stick do you place upon the fire? Which is the first oblation? To what did you sit near? What did you look toward? What is the subsequent oblation?

Having become what do you cause [the earth] to tremble? Having wiped the *sruva* spoon, why did you wipe it on the sacrificial grass-bundle (*kūrca*)? Having wiped the second [spoon], why did you place your hand to the south? Why did you consume the first [portion]? Why the second? Why, having stepped forward, did you drink? Why, having poured water into the *sruk* ladle, did you gaze at it? Why the second? Why the third? This [ladle].
"Did you sprinkle water toward the northern direction? Did you lead the waters around with the rear part [of the ladle]? Did you conclude [the rite] properly?
If you offered this Agnihotra knowing these things, then it was truly offered for you; but if you offered it without knowing them, then it was indeed unoffered for you.
He replied: "My Agnihotra cow is indeed Iḍā, the daughter of Manu; her calf is Vāyu; she is joined and let loose together as the Virāj."
The milk being milked belongs to the Aśvins; when milked, it belongs to the Viśvedevas;
while being brought [to the fire], it belongs to Vāyu; when placed on the fire, it belongs to Agni; when being stirred with the flame, it belongs to Indra and Agni;
when returned with water, it belongs to Varuṇa; and when being taken off [the fire], it belongs to Vāyu.
The [Soma] set out for Heaven and Earth; that being lifted up belongs to the Aśvins; that which has been lifted up belongs to the Viśve Devas;
that raised up for Mahādeva belongs to Vāyu; that being carried away belongs to Viṣṇu; and that which has been deposited belongs to Viṣṇu. 11.5.3.
[6] Now, the fuel-stick which I place upon the fire is the support of the oblations; by means of that first oblation, I have sent forth the gods.
That which I sat upon was dedicated to Bṛhaspati; by that I have established myself in both this world and the yonder world.
That which was my subsequent oblation, by that I have established myself in the heavenly world.
Now, when after offering I shake [the spoon], that is dedicated to Vāyu; and when, having wiped the *sruva* ladle, I place it on the grass-bundle (*kūrca*).

By wiping the plants and trees, I have gratified them; by wiping a second time and sitting down to the south with my hand, I have gratified the ancestors; by eating the first [portion], I have gratified myself; by eating the second, I have gratified offspring; then, by moving away and drinking water, I have gratified cattle; and by pouring water into the ladle—
With that [first sprinkling], I looked upon the serpents and the divine folk; with that second, I sent forth the Gandharvas and Apsarases;

and then, with that third, I sprinkled this direction upward, whereby I opened the door to the heavenly world. With what [water] I poured behind the Āhavanīya fire, I thereby bestowed rain for this world.

"Whatever I established, whatever was deficient on the earth, that I have filled up with this"—"Venerable sir, may this be common to us both," he said. 11.5.3 [8] Śauceya, having been instructed, said, "I shall indeed question you further, venerable sir. "Ask, Prācīnayogya," he replied.
He said, "At what time would those fires of yours be taken out, the vessels brought down, and you be about to offer the oblation? Then, for you—"

"If the Āhavanīya fire should go out, do you know the danger that arises here for one who offers oblations? "I know it," he replied. "Before long, the eldest son of one who does not know this would die; however, by means of these very sciences, I have crossed over. "What is known? What is the expiation? "The vital breath (prāṇa)."

"He has uttered an inspired utterance (*udāna*)," [thinking thus] one should offer an oblation in the *gārhapatya* fire; that itself is the expiation. "I would not commit that sin," [thinking thus]. "Venerable sir, this is common to us both," he said. 11.5.3. Śauceya, having been instructed, said, "I shall indeed question the venerable one further. "Ask, O Prācīnayogya," he replied. He (Śauceya) spoke:

"At that very time, when the *gārhapatya* fire has gone out, do you know that danger which arises for one who offers oblations here? "I know it," he replied. "The master of the house of one who does not know this would die before long;
however, by means of these sciences (*vidyās*), I have crossed over. "What is known? What is the expiation? "The *udāna* [breath]."

"He has gone into the vital breath; I shall offer an oblation into the Āhavanīya fire—this indeed is the expiation, I will not commit that sin. "Venerable sir, let us do this together," said Śauceya. Being thus informed, Śauceya said, "I shall ask you further, venerable sir. "Ask then, Prācīnayogya," he replied.
"If at that very time the fire for the ancestral rites (*anvāhāryapacana*) were to follow after this [sacrificial] fire, do you know what fear there is for one who offers oblations here?
"I know it," he said. "Before long, all the cattle of him who does not know this would perish."
"But perhaps I have crossed over by means of the *vidyās* alone. "What was known? What is the expiation?
"The *vyāna* has entered even the *udāna*. "One should offer an oblation in the *gārhapatya* fire; that indeed is the expiation. One should not commit that transgression.
"Venerable sir, let this be common to us both," he said. 11.5.3 [11]
Śauceya was informed, "I shall indeed question the Blessed One. [Prācīnayogya said,] "Ask, Prācīnayogya. He (Prācīnayogya) said:

"If at that very time all your fires should go out, do you know what danger there is for one who offers oblations? [Śauceya] replied, "I know it. [Prācīnayogya said,] "Before long, the lineage of one who does not know this would become heirless."

"Could it be that I have indeed crossed over by means of the *vidyās*? "What has been known? What is the expiation (*prāyaścitti*)? "Having churned the fire after a long time, I would take out the *āhavanīya* fire toward whichever direction the wind blows and offer a *vāyavyā* oblation.
That [knowledge] is my perfected *agnihotra*, for it belongs to all the deities; indeed, Vāyu is all [the deities]."
"Even the elements go into the wind and are released from it again; that itself is the atonement. One should not commit that sin.
"Venerable sir, this is common to us both," he said. 11.5.3.
Śauceya, having been instructed, said, "I shall indeed question the venerable one further. "Ask, Prācīnayogya," he replied. He said:

"In that very situation, when all the fires should go out while it is windless—at that time, do you know what danger arises for one who offers oblations here? "I know it," he said. "He who does not know this would see only what is unpleasant in this world and what is unpleasant in the next; but by means of these sciences, I have indeed crossed over. "What [is that]? he asked.

"What is the atonement for this? he asked. "In the past, after rubbing the fire for a long time and drawing out the Āhavanīya fire facing east, one should sit behind the Āhavanīya and say: 'I alone shall drink this; may my Agnihotra, which belongs to all the gods, be successful. For indeed, all beings merge into the Brāhmaṇa, and from the Brāhmaṇa they are released again.'"

"That itself is the atonement; one should not commit that offense again, nor should one say, 'I did not know this,'" he said. 11.5.3 [13] Śauceya, having been instructed, said, "Here are pieces of wood for the fire; come, let me attend upon you, O Blessed One. He said, "If you had not spoken thus, your head would have fallen off. Come, enter as a student. "So be it," he replied, and he initiated him. To him he [taught] this—
He uttered a speech more sorrowful than grief; therefore, one should speak only the truth.

(11.5.4) "I have come for the life of a *brahmacārī*," he says; this is how he offers himself to the *brahman*. "May I be a *brahmacārī*," he says; this is how he entrusts himself to the *brahman*. Then he asks him: "Who..."
"Your name is Ka," [he says]. Prajāpati indeed is Ka; thus, having made him belong to Prajāpati, he initiates him.
Then he takes his hand, saying: "Indra is the student, Agni is your teacher; I am your teacher, O so-and-so. These two are indeed the most excellent and most powerful deities.
By means of these two most excellent and most powerful deities, he entrusts him [the student]; thus his *brahmacārī* does not suffer any affliction whatsoever, nor does he who knows this. 11.5.4.
[3] Then he entrusts him to the beings: "I entrust you to Prajāpati; I entrust you to the god Savitṛ."

"I entrust him"—these two indeed are the most excellent and most sublime deities; by means of these very most excellent and most sublime deities, he entrusts him. Thus, his student does not encounter any misfortune whatsoever, nor does he who knows this. 11.5.4. [4]
"From the waters, from the plants, I entrust you"—thus he entrusts him to the waters and to the plants.
"To heaven and earth, I entrust you"—thus he entrusts him to these two, heaven and earth, over which all this world rests. "To all beings, I entrust you for safety"—thus he [entrusts him].
"He entrusts him to all beings for their protection; thus his student does not suffer any affliction whatsoever, nor does he who knows this.
(11.5.4) "Thou art a student," he says; thereby he entrusts him to the Brahman. "Drink water," he says; for water is indeed immortality.

"Drink the waters, eat the nectar"—this is what he says to him thereby. "Perform the work"—work is indeed vigor; thus he says to him, "Exert vigor. "Place the fuel"—this is what he says to him, "Kindle yourself with brilliance and spiritual luster. "Do not sleep"—this is what he says to him, "Do not die."
Then he says, "Eat water. Water is indeed immortality; thus he says to him, "Eat immortality. He thereby encloses him on both sides with immortality.

Thus, the student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) does not suffer any affliction, nor does he who knows this. Then he recites the Sāvitrī verse to him. Formerly, they used to recite it after a year had passed; it is commensurate with the year.
"Indeed, embryos are born; once he is born, we shall place speech into him. 11.5.4[7].
Then, after six months—for there are six seasons in a year, and embryos are born in accordance with the measure of a year—"once he is born, we shall place speech into him. 11.5.4[8].

Now, on the twenty-fourth day: there are indeed twenty-four half-months in a year; embryos are born when they have reached the measure of a year. [The thought is: "While he is already born, let us bestow speech upon him. Now, on the twelfth day: there are indeed twelve months in a year; it is equal to a year.
Now, in six days there are six seasons of the year; this is the attainment of the year.

Now, in three days there are three seasons of the year; this is the attainment of the year. Regarding this, they also sing a verse: "The teacher becomes pregnant when he places his right hand [upon her]; on the third [day], he..."
"He is born together with the Sāvitrī, O Brāhmaṇa"—thus one should indeed recite it immediately for a Brāhmaṇa. For the Brāhmaṇa belongs to Agni, and Agni is born immediately;
therefore, one should recite it immediately for a Brāhmaṇa.
Now, some recite this Sāvitrī as an Anuṣṭubh verse, saying, "The Anuṣṭubh is speech; thus we place speech within him."

Therefore, one should not do it in that way; for if someone were to say of him in that case, "Ah! He has swallowed his speech; he will become mute," it would very likely come to pass exactly so. Therefore, one should recite this very Gāyatrī Sāvitrī [to him].
Now, some indeed recite it to one who is standing or sitting to the south; one should not do it in that way, for if someone were to say of him in that case—
He should say, "Verily, this one has produced a bulb; he will become a bulb. For it is possible that it would indeed be so.
Therefore, he should recite the invitatory verse while looking toward the west from the east.
He recites it in three sections, for there are three vital breaths: the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the up-breath (*udāna*), and the through-breath (*vyāna*).

The *vyāna* breath places those very [breaths] within him. Then he recites by half-verses; for there are these two breaths, the *prāṇa* and the *udāna*, and thus he places both the *prāṇa* and the *udāna* within him. Then he recites the whole [verse];
for this breath is indeed one, the whole, and thus he places the entire breath within him. 11.5.4. [16]

Regarding this they say: "One should not engage in sexual intercourse after having initiated a Brahmin into studentship (*brahmacarya*). For he who enters upon studentship becomes an embryo; [one should not do so] lest one should cause this Brahmin to be born from spilled semen.
Regarding this they also say: "One may indeed engage in it at will. For these creatures are of two kinds: divine and human. These..."

These human beings are born from procreation; the divine beings are the *chandas* (Vedic meters), and he generates them from his mouth. From there he generates this [the student]; therefore, he may indeed eat as he desires. Regarding this they say: "One who is a religious student (*brahmacārī*) must not eat honey, for honey is the supreme essence of plants."

"I shall not go to the end of this food," he said. Then Śvetaketu Āruṇeya, while still a student, used to say as he was eating honey: "This honey which remains is indeed the residue of the threefold knowledge;
it is the essence of that for which such a residue remains. Just as one would recite a *ṛc*, a *yajus*, or a *sāman*, so too is that [which he says]. Thus it is for one who knows this.

The learned one, being a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), eats honey; therefore, he may eat it according to his desire. When the gods were ascending to the heavenly world, the Asuras obstructed them with darkness. They said, "There is indeed no way to repel this other than through a sacrificial session (*sattra*); come, let us perform a sacrificial session!"

They undertook the Sattra sacrifice consisting of a hundred Agniṣṭomas; by it they drove away as much darkness as one could see while sitting. In the same way, with the Śatokthya, they drove away as much darkness as one could see while standing. 11.5.5 [3]
They said, "We have indeed dispelled the darkness, yet not entirely. Come, let us go back to Prajāpati, our father.
Having approached Prajāpati, their father, they said, "O Venerable One, the Asuras have indeed obstructed the upward path to the heavenly world for us with darkness."

We entered upon the Śatāgniṣṭoma sacrificial session; we dispelled as much darkness as one could see while sitting. In the very same way, with the Śatokthya, we dispelled as much darkness as one could see while standing. O Venerable One, please instruct us further.
"Just as [the gods], having struck away the darkness and having struck away all evil, shall find the heavenly world," [they said].
He replied, "Indeed, you have come by means of two sacrifices that do not encompass all rites; namely, the Agniṣṭoma and the Ukthya.
Enter upon the sacrificial session (*sattra*) consisting of one hundred and more *Atirātras*; thereby, having struck away the darkness of the Asuras and having struck away all evil..."
"You shall know the heavenly world," [he said].

They undertook the Sattra sacrifice of a hundred Atirātras; by means of it, having struck away the darkness of the Asuras and having struck away all evil, they came to know the heavenly world. Among them, however, while there were still fifty days remaining, they completed the Rātrisāman chants for each day.
The *ahar-sāmans* follow the night.
They said, "We have indeed become bewildered; we do not understand. Come, let us go back to our father Prajāpati.
Having gone back to their father Prajāpati, they said, "The *rātri-sāmans* belong to the night, yet for us they occur during the day."
"O wise one, learned and steadfast, instruct us who are deluded regarding sacrifices.
To them he sang this: "As if a stronger man, having followed after [a weaker one], has driven him from his own place, so the sacrifice is not extended from that point."

"The *prātaranuvāka* belonging to the Aśvins, while it was being recited, drove you from your place; because it drove you from your place, though you are wise, you acted like those who are not. Approach that *praśāstṛ* slowly and do not recite against him. They said, "How, O Venerable One, is it recited? How is it not recited against? He replied, "Where..."

While the Hotṛ recites the Śastra for the Aśvins, he should reach the conclusion of the Āgneya ritual portion belonging to the Gāyatrī metre; then the Pratiprasthātṛ, having carried around the Vasatīvarī waters, should cause the Maitrāvaruṇa to begin the Prātaranuvāka at the two Havirdhāna sheds—
the Hotṛ recites it aloud, while the other follows along in a low voice, as if whispering.
"Therefore, one does not attain speech by means of speech, nor does one attain the *candas* by means of the *candas*.

(11.5.5.11) When the *prātaranuvāka* has been concluded, having offered the *upāṃśu* and *antaryāma* cups according to their proper place, he places the filter to be squeezed into the *droṇakalaśa*. Having performed the rites with the *tiro'hnaya* cups, they turn back and return.

"Consume only the *tirohna* portions; then, having completed the *yajñapuccha* in due order, having drawn the cups that come after the *antaryāma*, having offered the oblation of the drops (*vipruṣ*), and having chanted the *saṃtani* with the *bahiṣpavamāna*, you may proceed with the day itself. 11.5.5. [12]

Regarding this, there are these verses: "The wise ones, who are learned and perform the *śatakratu* sacrifice, have abandoned darkness by means of four harnessed Saindhava horses; they are the gods who performed the sacrificial session (*sattra*).
(11.5.5) For here, four are indeed harnessed: two *hotṛ*s and two *adhvaryu*s; praise them like the jaws of a powerful horse.
The wise, fashioning the ends of the days, interweave them; we do not understand the sacrificial thread stretched out by these Dānavas.

They bewilder us; they pour out the work of the former day and spread it over with the latter day. The wisdom of the deities is difficult to discern: the Soma-pressings are interwoven with the Soma-juices.
"They float, they constantly sprinkle their equals, like horses carrying wood; full jars of flowing liquor at Janamejaya’s abode"—with these words, the Asuras and Rakṣasas departed.

(11.5.6) There are indeed five great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*); they are themselves the great sacrificial sessions (*mahāsattrāṇi*): the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*), the sacrifice to men (*manuṣyayajña*), and the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*).
"The sacrifice to the gods and the sacrifice to Brahman" (11.5.6).

Day after day one should offer the *bali* to the beings; thus one completes this sacrifice to the beings (*bhūtayajña*). Day after day one should give [alms], even if it be only as much water as fits in a vessel; thus one completes this sacrifice to men (*manuṣyayajña*). Day after day...

One should offer the *svadhā* with water from a vessel; thus one completes this sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*). One should offer the *svāhā* with wood; thus one completes this sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*).
Now follows the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*): the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is indeed the sacrifice to Brahman. Of this very sacrifice to Brahman—

Speech is the *juhū* ladle, mind the *upabhṛt*, sight the *dhruvā*, intelligence the *sruva*, truth the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), and the heavenly world the ascent. Indeed, whatever extent of this earth one might conquer by giving it filled with wealth,
three times that extent, and even more— inexhaustible— does he conquer who, knowing this, studies his own sacred texts daily.

Therefore, the *svādhyāya* should be studied. 11.5.6. [4] These *ṛc*s are indeed milk-offerings for the gods. He who, knowing this, studies the *ṛc*s as his daily *svādhyāya*, satisfies the gods with milk-offerings; they, being satisfied, satisfy him in return.

With security and well-being, with vital breath, with semen, with their whole self, and with all meritorious riches, they carry the svadhā offerings toward the ancestors as streams of clarified butter and streams of honey. 11.5.6 [5]

The sacrificial formulas (yajūṃṣi) are indeed the oblations of clarified butter (ājyāhuti) for the gods. He who, knowing this, studies the sacrificial formulas as his daily private recitation (svādhyāya), thereby satisfies the gods with oblations of clarified butter. They, being satisfied, satisfy him in turn with security of possession (yogakṣema) and with vital breath. 11.5.6. [6]

The Sāmans are indeed oblations of Soma for the gods. He who, knowing this, studies the Sāmans as his daily private recitation (svādhyāya), satisfies the gods with oblations of Soma. They, being satisfied, satisfy him in turn with security of possession (yogakṣema) and with vital breath. 11.5.6. [7]

The Atharvāṅgirases are indeed fat-offerings to the gods. He who, knowing this, studies the Atharvāṅgirases as his daily private recitation, satisfies the gods with fat-offerings. They, being satisfied, satisfy him with security of possession and vital breath. 11.5.6 [8]
These instructions, the sciences, the dialogues, the *itihāsas* and *purāṇas*, the *gāthās*, and the *nārāśaṃsīs* are indeed honey-offerings to the gods.

He who, knowing this, studies daily as his private recitation the instructions, the sciences, the dialogues, the *itihāsas* and *purāṇas*, the *gāthās*, and the *nārāśaṃsīs*, does so with honey-offerings alone.
Thus he satisfies the gods, and they, being satisfied, satisfy him with security of possession and vital breath.

Of this very sacrifice to Brahman, there are four *vaṣaṭ*-calls: when the wind blows, when it lightens, when it thunders, and when it crashes. Therefore, one who knows this [should recite] while the wind blows, while it lightens...

One should indeed study while it thunders and while it lightens, so that there may be no failure of the *vaṣaṭ* calls. He is surely released from returning death and attains identity with Brahman. Even if he should be unable to do much, he should at least study a single word of the Veda; thus he is not deprived of the world of beings. 11.5.7.1 [1]

Now, therefore, follows the praise of private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). One becomes fond of private study and the recitation of the Vedas; with a disciplined mind, one becomes independent of others and accomplishes one's goals day by day. One sleeps happily and becomes the supreme physician for oneself. Furthermore, there is restraint of the senses, delight in solitude, the perfection of wisdom, fame, the ripening of the world [through teaching], and wisdom itself.
When these four qualities increase, they bring about the perfection of a Brāhmaṇa:
Brahmanical status, appropriate conduct, fame, and the ripening of the world. And when the world is ripened, it sustains the Brāhmaṇa through four qualities:
by honoring him, by giving to him, by not treating him with contempt, and by not harming him. 11.5.7 [2]

Whatever labors there may be between heaven and earth, the private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is indeed their highest point and ultimate goal for one who, knowing this, studies his private recitation. Therefore, the private recitation must be studied. Whatever meters he studies as his private recitation, by each of those very [meters] does it [accomplish] for him.
The sacrifice is performed for one who, knowing this, studies his own sacred text (*svādhyāya*);
therefore, one's own sacred text must be studied.
Even if one is anointed, adorned, well-fed, and lying on a comfortable bed, if he studies his own sacred text, [it is as if he has performed the sacrifice]. 11.5.7. [4]
"Truly, he who, knowing this, studies his own portion of the Veda (svādhyāya), burns even unto the tips of his nails;
therefore, one's own portion of the Veda should be studied.
"The Ṛg-verses are indeed honey, the Sāman-chants are indeed clarified butter, and the Yajus-formulas are indeed nectar. And as for this [person]..."
"He studies the *vākovākya* (dialogues); these two are indeed the rice cooked with milk and the rice cooked with meat.
[11.5.7.6] "Verily, he who, knowing this, studies the *ṛc* verses as his daily private recitation (*svādhyāya*), satisfies the gods with honey.
They, being satisfied, satisfy him with all desires and all enjoyments. [11.5.7.7]
Verily, he who, knowing this, studies the Sāmans daily as his private recitation, satisfies the gods with clarified butter; they, being satisfied, [protect him]. 11.5.7.
[8] Verily, he who, knowing this, studies the Yajus formulas daily... satisfies the gods with ambrosia.

Those [deities] are satisfied by him who, knowing this, studies his daily lesson (*svādhyāya*) day after day—whether it be the dialogues (*vākovākya*), the *Itihāsas*, or the *Purāṇas*. Being satisfied, they satisfy him with milk-rice and meat-rice. (11.5.7.9–10)

The waters go, the sun goes, the moon goes, and the stars go. Just as these deities would not function if they did not move, even so does a Brāhmaṇa become on that day when he does not study his sacred lesson.
Therefore, one's own lesson must be studied; therefore, one should at least recite a Ṛg-verse, a Yajus-formula, a Sāman-chant, a Gāthā, or a Kuṇyā.
Or he should utter [the syllable "Om"] for the sake of not interrupting his vow.

11.5.8.[1] Prajāpati alone was this universe in the beginning. He desired, "May I exist; may I procreate. He exerted himself and practiced austerity. From him, thus exerted and having practiced austerity, the three worlds were created: earth, the intermediate space, and heaven. 11.5.8.[2]
He heated these three worlds; from them, thus heated, three lights were born: Agni, he who blows here (Vāyu), and Sūrya.
He heated these three lights; from them, thus heated, the three Vedas were born: from Agni, the Ṛgveda.
From the wind came the Yajurveda; from the sun, the Sāmaveda. He heated these three Vedas; from them, thus heated, three pure essences were born:
"Bhūḥ" from the Ṛgveda, "Bhuvaḥ" from the Yajurveda, and "Svaḥ" from the Sāmaveda. With the Ṛgveda alone they performed the office of the Hotṛ priest.

With the Yajurveda he performed the duties of the Adhvaryu; with the Sāmaveda, the Udgītha; and with that which is the essence (*śukra*) of the threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*), he performed the office of the Brahman priest.
Then it departed upward.
(11.5.8) Those gods said to Prajāpati: "If our sacrifice [is deficient] from the Ṛgveda, or from the Yajurveda, or from the Sāmaveda..."
"Whose [part] has been injured? Let us heal it.
He said: "If it is injured on account of the *ṛc*, take four spoonfuls of clarified butter and offer them in the *gārhapatya* fire;
if on account of the *yajus*, take four spoonfuls of clarified butter and offer them in the *āgnīdhrīya* fire or in the *anvāhāryapacana* fire."

In a *havis*-sacrifice, if there is a discrepancy regarding the Sāman, one should take four spoonfuls of clarified butter and offer them into the Āhavanīya fire with the word "Svar. If, however, the error is unknown, one should recite all [the formulas] and offer them into the Āhavanīya fire. Thus, one heals the Ṛgveda by means of the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda by means of the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda by means of the Sāmaveda; it is just as one joins joint to joint.

He truly joins together in this way who heals with these [verses]; but he who heals with something other than these is like one who would try to join what is broken with what is broken, or like one who would place poison upon a wound. Therefore, one should appoint as Brahman only one who knows this, and not one who does not know this. 11.5.8. [7]

Regarding this they say: "Since the office of the Hotṛ is performed with the Ṛgveda, that of the Adhvaryu with the Yajurveda, and the Udgītha with the Sāmaveda, then by what is the office of the Brahman priest performed?
One should reply: "By means of this triple knowledge (the three Vedas).
This Aṃśu cup is indeed Prajāpati; it is his very self, for Prajāpati is this self. And the Ādābhya cup is speech.
When he has drawn the *aṃśu* cup, he draws the *ādābhya* cup; having thus consecrated his very self, he establishes this speech within it.
Now, the *aṃśu* is indeed the mind and the *ādābhya* is speech; the *aṃśu* is the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and the *ādābhya* is the up-breath (*udāna*); the *aṃśu* is the eye.
The ear is *adābhya*; that these two cups are drawn is for the sake of allness, for completeness.

11.5.9.[3] Now, both the gods and the Asuras, the offspring of Prajāpati, were contending; they contended over this very sacrifice, over Prajāpati, saying, "This shall be ours! This shall be ours! 11.5.9.[4]
Then the gods, praising and toiling, went about; they saw this cup, this Adābhya; they drew it.
They cut off the pressings; they appropriated the entire sacrifice and excluded the Asuras from the sacrifice. 11.5.9. [5]
They said, "We have indeed deceived them," and because of that it is called *adābhya*. [Others said,] "They did not deceive us," and because of that it is called *adābhya*.

Speech, indeed, is *adābhya*; this speech is undeceivable, and for that reason also it is *adābhya*. Verily, in this way he appropriates the entire sacrifice of his hateful rival; in this way he [overcomes] his hateful rival.
He excludes from all sacrifice and casts him out who knows this thus.
11.5.9.[6] With the very same vessel with which he draws the *aṃśu* cup, having poured water from the *nigrābhya*s into that same vessel, he draws these *aṃśu* shoots into it. 11.5.9.[7]

"You are taken with a support; I take you for Agni, whose metre is the Gāyatrī"—thus he extracts the Gāyatra [cup], which is the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*). "I take you for Indra, whose metre is the Triṣṭubh"—thus he extracts the Traiṣṭubha [cup], which is the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*). "For the All-gods (*viśve devāḥ*)... [he takes you].
"I take the Jagac-candas," he says; thus the third pressing belongs to the Jagatī, and so he excludes that third pressing.
"The Anuṣṭubh is your song of praise," he says; for whatever is above the pressings belongs to the Anuṣṭubh, and so he excludes that as well.
He does not press it, for the pressing-stone is a thunderbolt and the Ādābhya is speech; he does this lest he strike speech with the thunderbolt.
"May I strike down," [he says].
11.5.9.[8] He shakes the stalks themselves: "In the flight of the Vr̥śīs, I shake you; in the flight of the Kukūnanās, I shake you;
in the flight of the Bhandanās, I shake you; in the flight of the most intoxicating ones, I shake you."

‘In flight I shake thee, most honeyed in flight; in flight I shake thee’—these indeed are the divine waters. Thus, with both those which are divine waters and these which are human, he places sap in him. 11.5.9. [9]

"I shake thee, the bright one, in the bright," for he indeed shakes this bright one in the bright; "in the form of the day, in the rays of the sun"—thereby he shakes him both in the form of the day and in the rays of the sun. "The lofty form of the bull shines brightly"—this, indeed, is the lofty form of the bull.

"He who shines forth as this bright one is pleasing; the bright [Soma] is the precursor of the bright, Soma is the precursor of Soma"—thus he makes the bright one the precursor of the bright, Soma the precursor of Soma. "O Soma, that invincible name of thine which is watchful—for that thee I draw thee. For this indeed is his invincible name, which is watchful.
Or rather, that which is speech—he thereby takes hold of that very speech.
11.5.9. Then, having gone out, he offers an oblation with the formula: "To thee, O Soma, for Soma, svāhā! Thus he offers Soma itself to Soma;
in this way, he does not let go of speech into the fire. Then he breathes over the gold; it is indeed that same [speech].
His kinsman is only as great as his sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
11.5.9 [12] Then he gathers the stalks (*aṃśu*) once again: "O divine Soma, you who desire us, go to the beloved abode of Agni;
O divine Soma, you who have self-control, go to the beloved abode of Indra; O divine Soma, you who are our friend, [go to the beloved abode] of all the gods."
"Go to the beloved path!"—by this he draws forth the pressings;
he thereby causes them to swell again and makes them free from weariness. With those pressings, being free from weariness, they extend the sacrifice.
Bhṛgu Vāruṇi, indeed, surpassed his father Varuṇa in knowledge. Varuṇa became aware of that.
"Indeed, he thought, 'I am superior through my knowledge.
He said, "My son, go toward the east; having seen what you see there, go toward the south; having seen what you see there, go toward the west; having seen what you see there, go toward the north."

"Whatever you see, having seen that, proceed from these two toward the northern intermediate direction; whatever you see there, report it to me. He set out from there toward the east. There he saw men [beating] men limb by limb.
As they were cutting him up joint by joint and distributing him, saying, "This is yours, this is mine," he said, "Alas!

O men, these men have indeed cut me apart joint by joint and divided me. They replied, "In that way, indeed, these [men] attended upon us in yonder world; therefore, we shall now attend upon them here in return. Thus he spoke.

He said, "Is there here an expiation? "There is," [he replied]. "What is it? "Your father knows that. He then set out toward the south with sacrificial gifts. He came upon men who were having men cut their joints apart, joint by joint, and dividing them joint by joint, saying, "This is yours, this is mine. He said, "Alas, Bhīṣma!"

"O men, these men here have cut our joints apart and divided them joint by joint! They replied, "In this very way these [men] attended upon us in yonder world; let us now attend upon them here in return. He said, "Is there an atonement for this?"—"There is," they said. "What is it?"—"Only your father knows," he said. (11.6.1)
He departed from that very place toward the west.
There he saw men being eaten by men who were sitting silently, while those being eaten themselves were sitting silently. He said, "Alas, O sirs!
Men are indeed eating these men who are sitting silently, while the eaters themselves are sitting silently. They replied, "Indeed, it is so."
"These [ancestors] served us in yonder world; let us now serve them here," he said. He replied, "Is there a remedy for this?
"There is," they said. "What is it? "Only your father knows.
Thereupon, he departed from that very place toward the north. He went among men, making men cry out.
While they were crying out as they were being devoured, he said, "Alas, O men!
These men are indeed making these men cry out as they devour them. They replied, "Indeed, it is thus that these [beings] are devouring us.
Then he went from there toward the northern intermediate direction between those two previous ones; there were two women.
Between Kalyāṇī and Atikalyāṇī stood a man, dark-complexioned, with reddish-brown eyes, holding a staff in his hand.
Upon seeing him, he was seized by fear; he fled and hid himself. His father said to him, "Study your sacred recitation!
Why do you not study your sacred recitation? He replied, "What shall I study? There is nothing. This, indeed...
Varuṇa perceived:

"I have seen them. He said: "Those whom you saw in the eastern direction—men by men, their joints severing joint by joint and distributing them, saying 'This is yours, this is mine'—they were indeed the lords of the forest (trees)."
He was the trees; in that he places a fuel-stick of wood, he thereby wins the trees and thereby conquers the world of the trees. 11.6.1.
[9] Now, as for those men whom you saw in the southern quarter—men by men, their joints joint by joint.
"Those who were dividing the sacrificial cake joint by joint, saying, 'This is yours, this is mine,' became cattle.
Therefore, when one offers with milk, one thereby wins cattle; thereby one conquers the world of cattle.
"Now, as for those men whom you saw in the western direction—"
The men who were sitting silently were being devoured by those who were also sitting silently; they indeed became plants.
When you light it up with grass, by that you win the plants; by that you conquer the world of the plants. 11.6.1.
Now, as for those men whom you saw in the northern direction making men cry out—
Being devoured by those crying out, they indeed became the waters. In that he brings back the waters, he thereby secures the waters; thereby he conquers the world of the waters. 11.6.1.
Now, as for those two women whom you saw—the beautiful one and the exceedingly beautiful one—that which was the beautiful one is faith (*śraddhā*), and that...

In that he offers the first oblation, thereby he wins faith; thereby he conquers faith. Now, that which follows is unfaith; in that he offers the second oblation, thereby he wins unfaith; thereby he conquers unfaith. 11.6.1. [13]
Now, that man who stood between them—dark-skinned, with reddish-brown eyes, and holding a staff in his hand—was indeed Anger.
When he pours water into the offering-ladle and pours it out, by that he secures Anger; by that he conquers Anger.
He who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra, conquers everything and secures everything. 11.6.2.1.

Janaka of Videha met with certain Brahmins who were traveling about: Śvetaketu Āruṇeya, Somaśuṣma Sātyayajñi, and Yājñavalkya. He said to them, "In what manner, pray, do you offer the Agnihotra? 11.6.2 [2]
Śvetaketu Āruṇeya said, "O Emperor, I offer two inexhaustible *gharma* oblations, overflowing with glory, into one another. How is that? The sun is indeed the *gharma*;
I offer it into the fire in the evening. Fire is indeed the *gharma*; I offer it into the sun in the morning. "What becomes of him who does so? [he asked].
"One who offers oblations in this manner becomes possessed of uninterrupted prosperity and fame; he wins union with and residence in the same world as these two deities.
Then Śomaśuṣma Sātyayajñi said: "O Emperor, I offer only into brilliance; I offer into brilliance. How so?"
"That"—the sun is indeed brilliance; "I offer that in the fire in the evening. "Fire," indeed, is brilliance; "I offer that in the sun in the morning.
"What becomes of him who offers thus? "He becomes brilliant, glorious, and an eater of food; he wins union with and residence in the same world as these two deities. 11.6.2. [4]
Then Yājñavalkya said: "When I lift the fire, I am indeed lifting up the Agnihotra itself;

for all the gods follow the sun as it sets, and seeing that fire of mine lifted up, they turn back toward it. Then, having washed the vessels, having placed them in order, and having caused the Agnihotra cow to be milked..."
"Beholding that which beholds, I satisfy it"—this, Yājñavalkya, you have not investigated as the nearest [aspect] of the Agnihotra.

"I give you a hundred cows," he said. "But indeed, you have not told me its departure, nor its path, nor its foundation, nor its satisfaction, nor its return, nor the one who rises up to meet it in the world. Having said this, he mounted his chariot and drove away.

[He] did so. 11.6.2.[5] They said, "This kinsman of a king has indeed spoken over us; come, let us challenge him to a theological debate. Yājñavalkya said, "We are indeed Brāhmaṇas, while he is a kinsman of a king. If [he challenges] this man..."
"Whom shall we conquer? Whom have we conquered? they asked.

Then, if that kinsman of the ruling class (rājanyabandhu) should defeat us, they would say, "O Brāhmaṇas, you have been defeated; yield this [to him]! And so they recognized his superiority. Then Yājñavalkya said:

He caused [the chariot] to drive after him as he was mounting the chariot, and he (Yājñavalkya) followed him. He (the King) said: "O Yājñavalkya, do you know the Agnihotra? "I know the Agnihotra, O Emperor," he replied. Indeed, these two oblations, once offered, rise up; they enter the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); the intermediate space itself is their *āhavanīya* fire.
They make the wind their fuel and the rays of light their bright oblation; they satisfy the intermediate space and then ascend from there.
They enter heaven; they make heaven itself the Āhavanīya fire, the sun the fuel, and the moon the [oblation].
The bright oblation satisfies you; from there it returns to you.
They enter this [earth]; they make this very earth their *āhavanīya* fire, and the fuel is the plants.
The bright oblation satisfies this [earth]; from there they rise up again.

They enter the person; they make his mouth the Āhavanīya fire, his tongue the fuel, and food the bright oblation. They satisfy the person. For one who knows this, when he eats, it becomes as if the Agnihotra has been offered by him. They then depart from there. 11.6.2. [10]

They enter the woman; they make her womb the Āhavanīya fire. The *dhārakā* is the fuel-stick; for this indeed is called *dhārakā*, by which Prajāpati supported his offspring. The *śukrā* is the oblation of semen;
with it they satisfy the woman. He who, knowing this, approaches a woman in union, has truly offered the Agnihotra.

"The son who is born from that becomes the world that rises up to meet him; this, Yājñavalkya, is the Agnihotra sacrifice, and there is nothing higher than this," he said. To him, Yājñavalkya granted a boon. He said, "Let the privilege of asking questions at will be mine regarding you, O Yājñavalkya. Thereupon Janaka became a Brāhmaṇa. 11.6.3. [1]
Janaka of Videha performed a sacrifice at which many gifts were distributed.
While bestowing a thousand cows, he said: "O Brahmins, let him who is the most learned in the Veda among you drive these away.
Yājñavalkya said, "They are already driven away toward us. They replied, "Are you indeed, Yājñavalkya, the most learned in the Veda?"

Thus he said: "Homage be to the most proficient in the Veda; we are merely seekers of cattle. They said, "Who will ask this question for us? He replied, "I, Vidagdha Śākalya. Having recognized him, he said, "Cākalya, have the Brahmins indeed made you their fire-drill?"

He said, "Yājñavalkya, how many gods are there? "Three hundred and three, and three thousand and three. "Yes," he said. "But how many gods are there really, Yājñavalkya? "Thirty-three. "Yes," he said. "But how many gods are there really, Yājñavalkya? "Three. "Yes," he said. "But how many gods are there really, Yājñavalkya? "Two. "Yes," he said.

“How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? “One and a half,” he said. “Yes,” he replied. “How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? “One,” he said. “Yes,” he replied. “Which are those three and three hundred, and three and three thousand? He said, “These are merely their powers; there are only thirty-three gods. “Which are those?”

"Thirty-three," [it is said]. Eight are the Vasus, eleven are the Rudras, and twelve are the Ādityas; those make thirty-one. Indra and Prajāpati make the thirty-three. (11.6.3) "Who are the Vasus? "Agni and Pṛthivī, Vāyu and Antarikṣa, Āditya and Dyau."

The moon and the stars—these are the Vasus, for they cause all this to dwell; because they cause all this to dwell (*vāsayante*), therefore they are called the Vasus. "Who are the Rudras? "These ten vital breaths in a person, with the self as the eleventh."
"When they depart from this mortal body, they cause one to weep; because they cause one to weep (*rodayanti*), they are therefore called Rudras.
"Who are the Ādityas? The twelve months of the year are these Ādityas, for they go along taking (*ādadānāḥ*) all this [world] away;
because they go along taking all this away, they are therefore called Ādityas."

"Who is Indra? Who is Prajāpati? "Indra is indeed the thunder, and Prajāpati is the sacrifice. "What is the thunder? "It is the lightning bolt. "What is the sacrifice? "It is the cattle. "What are those three gods? "These very three worlds; for within these all the gods reside. "Who are those two?"

"Two gods," he said—"food and breath. "Which one is the one-and-a-half? "This one who blows here. "Who is the one god? "Breath. He (the teacher) said: "You have questioned me about a deity that should not be questioned beyond its limit. Before the next new moon, you shall die; your bones shall not remain [to be collected]."

"Perhaps they will reach home," he thought; but he died right there. Thinking them to be robbers, others carried off his bones. Therefore, one should not be a reviler, for even one who knows this becomes an enemy. One performs the Paśubandha sacrifice. The Paśubandha is indeed cattle; in that he performs the Paśubandha sacrifice...

"Thinking, 'May I possess cattle,' one should sacrifice with that [offering] in the house, for it is said, 'In the house they bind cattle. Thinking, 'May I possess cattle,' one should sacrifice with that on good pasture, for it is said, 'On good pasture they bind cattle.
Indeed, the fires of the sacrificer wear out as he offers; when the fires wear out, the sacrificer follows after them, and following the sacrificer come both the house and the cattle. (11.7.1)

When he performs the animal sacrifice, he thereby makes the fires new again; following the renewal of the fires, the sacrificer, his household, and his cattle are renewed. Indeed, this becomes for him a ransom for the self that bestows long life.
For the fires of a sacrificer who offers oblations do indeed become fleshly; they meditate only upon the sacrificer, upon the sacrificer.

Others resolve upon or cook meat unfit for sacrifice on other fires; yet for them, there is no desire for meat other than this, nor for him to whom they belong. (11.7.1[3]) When he sacrifices with the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), he thereby ransoms his very self—with a hero for a hero, for he is a hero.

The victim is the hero, the sacrificer; and this, indeed, is the supreme food, namely meat. He thus becomes an eater of the supreme food. The year should not pass over him without his eating [the victim]; for the year is life—verily, he places that immortal life within himself. 11.7.2.1.

Indeed, one kind of animal sacrifice follows the model of the *haviḥ-yajña* (oblation sacrifices), while another follows the model of the *sava* (pressing sacrifices). That which is of the *haviḥ-yajña* type is that in which he introduces the vow (*vrata*), in which he leads forward the waters (*apaḥ praṇayati*), in which he pours out the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*), and in which he makes him step the Viṣṇu-steps (*viṣṇukrama*). Now, that which is of the *sava* type is that in which these [rites] are not performed. 11.7.2. [2]

Regarding this they say: "Is it an *iṣṭi*, or an animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), or a great sacrifice (*mahāyajña*)? One should say, "It is a great sacrifice. For at that time, one performed both the *iṣṭi* and the animal sacrifice; thus one should say to him, "You have performed this [great sacrifice]. Of that [sacrifice], the *prayāja*s are indeed the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), the *anuyāja*s are the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is the midday pressing (*mādhyandina*).
Now, some lead the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) away when the omentum has been offered. One should not do it in that way;
for if someone were to say of him then, "He has led the sacrificial gifts outside of the vital breaths; he has not strengthened the vital breaths; he is either blind," or...
"He will become lame, or deaf, or paralyzed on one side"—thus indeed would the Lord (Īśvara) be; 11.7.2[5].
He should act in this very way: when the *iḍā* of the sacrificial cake has been invoked, he should lead the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
For this vital breath in the middle is indeed connected with Indra; thus he makes this vital breath in the middle belong to Indra.
He makes [the sacrificer] capable through the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*). The midday pressing belongs to Indra, and it is at the midday pressing that the sacrificial gifts are led forth;
therefore, one should lead the sacrificial gifts only when the *iḍā* for the rice-cake has been invoked.
Regarding this they say: "O Adhvaryu, since there is no ritual bath (*avabhṛtha*) for one who is consecrated, where did he undergo consecration?"

Thus, up until the final purificatory bath (āvabhṛtha), the Adhvaryu, the Pratiprasthātṛ, the Hotṛ, the Maitrāvaruṇa, the Brahman, and the Āgnīdhra should support [the sacrifice]. For by these six is this Ṣaḍḍhotṛ [formula] constituted; having recited that Ṣaḍḍhotṛ formula, he offers one oblation.
Having made one offering, there are five [verses] with clarified butter: "The sky is the back, the atmosphere is the self, [and] the sacrifice with its limbs."

"O Lord of Speech, with bodies upon the earth, with unimpaired speech as the ladle, he has sent forth the divine Hotṛ-offering that prospers the gods in heaven, saying 'Svāhā!'—that indeed is the consecration.
Regarding this they say: "O Adhvaryu, since no *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) is possible for one who is consecrated..."
"Where will you lead him for the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*? "When they proceed with the heart-spike (*hṛdayaśūla*), that indeed is his avabhṛtha.
Madhuka Paiṅgya used to say: "Some perform the animal sacrifice without Soma, while others perform it with Soma.
Soma was indeed in heaven; Gāyatrī, having become a bird, carried him off. The leaf of his [wing] that fell became the *parṇa* tree."

"This state of being made of leaves," so it is said in this Brāhmaṇa, "is proclaimed. Some perform the animal sacrifice without Soma, while others perform it with Soma. He who makes a sacrificial post other than one of *pālāśa* wood performs the animal sacrifice without Soma;
whereas he who makes a sacrificial post of *pālāśa* wood performs the animal sacrifice with Soma."

Therefore, one should make the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) from *pālāśa* wood alone. That which has much heartwood is not conducive to cattle; therefore, one who desires cattle should not make such a post. But that which is easily split and soft is conducive to cattle; therefore, one who desires cattle should make such a post.

Now, that sacrificial post which, being crooked, has its top like a spike is called *kapotī*. He who makes such a post goes to that world before his full span of life. Therefore, one who desires long life should not make such a post.
Now, that post which is bent at the bottom, straight in the middle, and bent at the top—that is the form of hunger.
If one makes such a sacrificial post, his wives will be hungry; therefore, one who desires food should not make such a post.
But that which is bent at the bottom, straight in the middle, and bent at the top—that is the form of food.

Therefore, one who desires such food and drink should make a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) of that kind. When he is about to sacrifice with an animal and makes a sacrificial post one cubit long, he thereby conquers this world; then, when it is two cubits long, he thereby conquers the intermediate space; and then, when it is three cubits long, he thereby conquers the sky.

Now, he who [measures] four *aratnis* conquers the quarters by that means. This sacrificial post for the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) is indeed three *aratnis* or four *aratnis* long; but whatever is longer than that belongs to the Soma-sacrifice (*adhvara*).

Regarding this, they say: "Should one offer the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) or not? They say, "One should offer them," for these two portions of clarified butter are the eyes of the sacrifice.
"What would a man be without eyes? [he asks]. For as long as they do not exclude the sharer from his own share, he considers himself excluded;
but when they exclude him from his own share, then he considers himself excluded. When the Hotṛ recites this, "The Rakṣas is snared..."
"May he unite it"—thereby he separates it from its own portion. Indeed, when the animal is being slaughtered, its heat (śuc) enters the heart; from the heart it goes to the omentum (ūla).
If they were to cook the animal together with the heart, the heat would again spread back into the animal. Therefore, one should place it on a wooden splinter from the side.
Having cut it, he should cook it.

He spreads a layer of clarified butter; that makes the form of the earth. He places a piece of gold; that makes the form of fire. He places the omentum; that makes the form of the intermediate space. He places a piece of gold.

In that he makes it [the omentum] into the form of the sun, and then in that he bastes it from above, he makes it into the form of heaven. This omentum indeed becomes fivefold; the sacrifice is fivefold, the animal is fivefold, and there are five seasons in the year.
Therefore, the omentum becomes fivefold. 11.8.1.1.
"Just as, for example, this wheel of a chariot or the potter's wheel might spin without a fixed support, even so these worlds were unstable and without a foundation.
Then Prajāpati reflected: "How indeed might these worlds become stable and firmly established? He—
With these very mountains, rivers, and birds, he strengthened this earth; with rays and clouds, the intermediate space;
and with stars, the sky.
He uttered the word "mahaḥ" (greatness); cattle indeed are greatness; therefore, he for whom these [cattle] are many becomes great.

"Most abundantly indeed are they honored in his family; for many of these [ancestors] of his become [honored], and most abundantly indeed are they honored in his family. Therefore, if they should oppress him from his dwelling or cause him to depart, he should, after offering the Agnihotra, worship with the word 'maha' (greatness). He stands firm with offspring and cattle and does not fall from his dwelling. 11.8.2.1.

There are indeed four fires: the established, the drawn out, the cast forward, and the spread out. This very world is the established; the intermediate world is the drawn out; the sky is the cast forward; and the quarters are the spread out. Fire itself is the established; Vāyu is the drawn out; Āditya is the cast forward;
and Candramas is the spread out. The Gārhapatya fire is the established; the Āhavanīya fire is the drawn out; and then—

That fire which they lead forth from the Āhavanīya toward the east is the one that has been "cast forward" (*prahṛta*); and that which they bring northward for the cooking of the animal victim and for the by-offerings (*upayaj*) is the one that has been "spread out" (*vihṛta*).
Therefore, one should perform the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*) in the fire that has been cast forward. 11.8.3. [1]
Regarding this, they ask: "Of which deity should this animal sacrifice be? They say: "It should belong to Prajāpati.
For Prajāpati indeed beheld it first; therefore, this animal sacrifice should belong to Prajāpati alone.
Furthermore, they also say: "This animal sacrifice should belong to Sūrya," for that is why animals are bound at this time when the sun has set.
“They bind [the victims] one by one; otherwise, they would assemble in a single pen. Therefore, this animal sacrifice should belong to Sūrya alone,” so they say.
But then they also say: “This animal sacrifice should belong to Indra and Agni. These two deities indeed follow after all the gods.
If one who is afflicted performs the sacrifice, these two carry him across; if one performs a great sacrifice, these two carry him across. Therefore, this animal sacrifice belongs to Indra and Agni.”
"It may be so.
11.8.3.[4] The breath alone is the animal sacrifice; therefore, as long as one lives, no other has power over his animals, for they remain bound within him. 11.8.3.[5]
Prajāpati said to Agni, "Sacrifice with me; let me obtain you. He replied, "No. "Then speak to Vāyu," he said.

He spoke to Vāyu, "Sacrifice with me; let me obtain you. He replied, "No. "Then speak to Puruṣa," he said. He spoke to Puruṣa, "Sacrifice with me; let me obtain you. He replied, "No. "Then speak to the cattle," he said. He spoke to the cattle.

"Let me sacrifice with you; let me obtain you," he said. "No," they replied, "speak to Candramas. He spoke to Candramas: "Let me sacrifice with you; let me obtain you. "No," he replied, "speak to Āditya.
He spoke to Āditya: "Let me sacrifice with you; let me obtain you. "So be it," he replied. As for those who did not desire this, what indeed [was their lot]?
"May these [misfortunes] not befall you; whatever you may desire," he said, and "So be it," he replied, and he seized him. This animal of his was seized and slaughtered;
he gratified him with these *āprī* verses. Because he gratified him with these *āprī* verses, they are called *āpriyaḥ*.
Therefore, one should say of a slaughtered animal, "Wait but a moment. He...

As much of the world as one wins by performing the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha), so much does one win by this [rite]. 11.8.3.[6] The eastern quarter breathed after him with the words, "Breathe forth!"—it thereby bestowed the out-breath (prāṇa) upon him. The southern quarter breathed after him with the words, "Breathe across!"—it thereby bestowed the cross-breath (vyāna) upon him. The western...

The western quarter breathed upon it with "Exhale!"—it thereby placed exhalation within it. The northern quarter breathed upon it with "Inhale!"—it thereby placed inhalation within it. The upward quarter breathed upon it with "Equalize!"—it thereby placed the equalizing breath within it. Therefore, [one should breathe upon] a son...

When [the child] is born with the umbilical cord uncut, one should say to five Brahmins, "Breathe upon him! If he cannot find them, he himself should breathe upon him while walking around him. He attains a full lifespan and lives until old age. 11.8.3. [7] He took the breath from Agni; therefore, this [fire] does not burn unless it is blown upon or kindled, for its breath has been taken away.
He who knows this indeed takes away the breath of his hateful rival.
11.8.3.[8] He took away the form of the wind; therefore, people hear it as if it were flickering, yet they do not see it, for its form has been taken away.
He who knows this indeed takes away the form of his hateful rival. 11.8.3.[9]
He took away the mind of man; therefore they say, "May the divine mind protect you, not the human mind," for he has indeed taken his mind.
He who knows this takes away the mind of his hateful rival. 11.8.3.
[10] He took away the sight of cattle; therefore, even when they are looking about as it were, they do not truly perceive.
As soon as they sniff it, they know it; for their sight has indeed been taken away. He who knows this takes away the sight of his hateful rival. 11.8.3.
[11] He took away the luster of the moon; therefore, although these two are similar, the moon is the less bright.
For his light (*bhās*) has indeed been taken away; truly, he who knows this takes away the light of his hateful rival.
Because he took it away (*ādatta*), therefore he is called Āditya.
Now, a tiger killed the *samrāḍdughā* cow belonging to those whose householder was Keśin. He [Keśin] then addressed his fellow-sacrificers.
"What expiation is there for this? they asked. "There is no expiation for this," they replied;
"only Khaṇḍika Audbhāri knows the expiation for it, and he desires for you both such a thing as this and something even worse.
He said, "Charioteer, harness my horses; I shall go. If he tells me [the answer], I will complete [my studies]."
"If he kills me, he will scatter the sacrifice along with me.

Having yoked [his chariot], he set out and arrived. Seeing him, [the other] said: "Since these skins are used for deer, let us break their ribs and cook them; my black antelope skin is tied around my neck," and so on.

"Let him come to you unassailable," [the other said]. "No," he replied, "O Venerable One, a tiger has already killed my cow that yields all desires. If you tell me [the way], I shall complete it; but if you kill me, I shall be torn apart along with the interrupted sacrifice."
He said, "Let me invite those who are to be invited. Having invited them, he said to them:
"If I tell this to him, his offspring alone will possess this world, while I shall be one who has no share in the world.
But if I do not tell it to him, my own offspring will possess this world, and he will be one who has no share in the world."

"It will come to be," they said. "Do not say so, venerable sir; this world indeed belongs to the Kṣatriya," he replied. He said, "I shall certainly tell you; those nights are indeed more numerous. To him he spoke this: "Having offered the *spṛt* oblations, say, 'Offer another. That, O Sovereign, shall be your milch-cow."
"From the moon I sustain your mind, svāhā! From the sun I sustain your eye, svāhā! From the wind I sustain your breaths, svāhā!

From the quarters I sustain your hearing, svāhā! From the waters I sustain your blood, svāhā! From the earth I sustain your body, svāhā! Then he should say, "Offer another oblation; may she be a cow that milks for you, O Sovereign. Thereupon, indeed, he [became such].
He exhausted the descendants of Kaiśinī; even now, these very progeny are born in this manner.
